claude.via: Claude Code subagent (Agent tool), not the API

claude.reason: Nero is sent, tests his fate with arrows and a child's verse, then flees and converts: several actions and a decisive change, about a post-biblical figure.
Within Rabba's dictum, R. Yohanan's statement embeds a story of two families who set their meals wrongly and were uprooted (two actions, causal connection), as the expert ruled on this passage.
Akiva and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter: betrothal, her father's expulsion and vow, his years of study and return - multiple actions and change.
An incident before Rabbi: a man taken captive with his mother recounts it offhandedly and Rabbi permits her to marry a priest; narrated events plus a ruling as resolution.
Rav Pappa goes to write his son's marriage contract, Yehuda bar Mareimar comes out to greet him and takes leave at the door; a narrated sequence of actions opening a story that continues.
Mar Zutra's habitual practice followed by an objection and a ruling; the expert ruled this exact passage a bare description with no continuation.
A situation is cited and Abaye says what he would have done; no further narrated action or change follows, only legal discussion.
One-time eyewitness wonders (walking in ankle-deep fig honey, seeing the land of milk and honey); the expert accepted this Ketubot 111b eyewitness type in review and lists it.
The death of Rabbi: the Sages' fast and decree, the maidservant's prayer and thrown jug, his death, bar Kappara's report, the heavenly voice - many actions and change.
Giddul bar Re'ilai sends a divorce, the agent finds his wife weaving, she defers it, he rejoices: a sequence of actions and responses.
A bare report of Rav Zevid's ruling or practice with nothing following.

The Sages allot Nakdimon's daughter a perfume allowance and she replies with a barbed blessing; an incident with a ruling but the response is speech with some implied tension rather than further action.
An incident before Rabbi: a man taken captive with his mother recounts it offhandedly and Rabbi permits her to marry a priest; narrated events plus a ruling as resolution.
A man contracts with his sharecropper, rain then falls and makes the fourth watering unnecessary, and rabbis rule; an incident with a change followed by a ruling, like the cow case.
Geneiva, led out to execution, bequeaths 400 zuz to R. Avina - a narrated incident; the following segments are legal reasoning about it, not the story.
Rabbi on his deathbed summons his sons, who enter, and gives his testament; segment 3 is the Gemara's commentary on his words and is excluded.
A woman taken as security in Ashkelon, distanced by her family, witnesses testify, and the Sages rule: narrated incident with response, quoted here by the Talmud.
Purely legal discussion of Shmuel's rulings and a mishna; no event narrated.
A gentile announces Hasa drowned, Rav Nahman exclaims, Hasa's wife goes and remarries and no one protests: actions and change, followed by Rav Ashi's inference.
Rav Kahana brings a bill of divorce and asks Rav, who rules; coming before a rabbi and receiving a ruling with no other narrated action or change (the 50b limit).
An incident in Shihin: inherited mustard stalks, one breaks, nine kav found and its wood used to roof a booth - a narrated one-time wonder of the Ketubot 111b type the expert accepts.
A man sold his property to go to Eretz Yisrael but did not go, and Rav Ashi rules; an incident with actions and a change followed by a ruling, as in the cow case.
R. Elazar ascends to the Land, is ordained, is seated in the intercalation council, responding at each stage: successive events and change.
Ulla arrives and notices Rav Yehuda's unmarried son; the rest is dialogue with exegetical digressions and advice, mostly speech with mild tension and no event following.
A man throws a supposed bill of divorce among the barrels, a mezuza is found, and Rav Nahman rules: a narrated incident with actions followed by a ruling.
A narrated incident ('a certain man') with actions (picking dates, the woman comes and asks, he proposes, she answers) resolved by Rav Zevid's ruling; the R-C0 incident-plus-ruling shape.
A man comes to Rabbi Nehemya, shares his lentils and dies, and Nehemya reacts: several actions and a drastic change.
A man bequeaths his property, dies, Toviya comes to claim it, and Rabbi Yohanan rules: an incident with more than one action, followed by a ruling.
Rav Kahana is tempted, falls from the roof, is caught by Elijah and given dinars. Many actions and a change; Elijah appearing to a rabbi is read as in scope.
The rabbis' sitting and discussing is not a story, but they cite a terse incident (slaves refused, waited twelve months, were sold) as evidence. It is reported as a precedent, not narrated.
A full narrative: years of support, a demand, a lawsuit, defiance of the ruling, seizure of property, appeal to Rava, and further argument. Many actions, conflict and change.
A hypothetical legal dilemma, left unresolved; nothing happened.
Land is sold, a river is diverted through it, and the case goes before Ravina and then Rava: an incident with a real change, followed by rulings.
A man comes before Rabban Gamliel with a claim and gets an answer and a parable. As at Ketubot 50b, coming before a rabbi and being ruled on is all that is narrated.
A hypothetical legal case from a baraita (if people saw her...), with a tannaitic dispute; it is not an event that happened.
A teaching and Rav Hisda's sharp retort: ordinary rabbinic dialogue with no action or change, the passage Jeff ruled out on 2026-10-07.
A Roman courts a woman, makes her ill with the pomegranates, then cures her when she agrees to marry him: several actions and a change. A post-biblical figure, so in scope.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba meets Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying his grandson to synagogue, questions him, and changes his own habit from then on: an encounter that leads to a change.
Two first-person eyewitness vignettes (food brought, a share given, danger averted), cited as evidence for a ruling. Minimal action, and close to the open 'I myself saw' edge.
Rabbi Akiva moves the garden's entrance to block Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's tithe, and Elazar reacts: an action, its consequence and a response, with conflict.
A habit (weekly charity) followed by a one-time event: one day his wife delivers it, comes back and reports what she overheard.
Jeff's Ketubot 61a ruling: the pious man's habit of feeding the waiter first leads to a change, since Elijah speaks with him.
Segment 3 is an incident (the witnesses wrongly write 'Tefata') followed by a ruling. Segment 2 only alludes to an incident, and segment 4 is the Gemara's legal objection.
A scribe comes before Rabbi Ami and makes a claim, followed by a ruling and a scholarly exchange. No narrated action or change beyond coming before a rabbi (R-C0's limit at Ketubot 50b).
A legal dilemma and a dispute, then Rav Nahman's rebuke of Rav Anan. Ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, not conflict in R-C2's sense.
The martyrdom of the woman and her seven sons before the emperor: repeated actions, conflict, deaths and a divine voice. Post-biblical figures, so in scope.
A brief report that descendants remained in Sura and the Sages avoided them, mostly the Gemara explaining why. It is a sequel note, not a narrated incident.
Rav Yosef's planting practice prompts Abaye's halakhic challenge, a reply, and a reconsideration resting on Rav's practice: ordinary scholarly debate about a practice.
A man sells his mother's marriage contract, his mother dies, he contests the sale, and Rami bar Hama and Rava rule: an incident with several actions and a change, followed by a ruling.

A case comes before Rabbi Yohanan; his answer exposes that Rabbi Elazar had quoted him without attribution, and Reish Lakish looks at Elazar harshly and rebukes him. A narrated reaction and a realisation beyond the speech.

Rabbi Elazar teaches without attribution, Rabbi Yohanan becomes angry, colleagues try and fail to appease him, Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi succeeds: multiple actions, conflict and change. The closing question about Yohanan's reason is Gemara commentary (R-B4) but sits in the same segment as the story's end.
A halakhic objection and response between Rav Yosef, Abaye and Rava; ordinary scholarly dialogue with no narrated event.
On Rabbi's funeral day a Divine Voice speaks, the launderer who missed it hears, throws himself from the roof and dies, and a second Voice grants him the World-to-Come: several actions and a change.
Hillel's habitual provision for the impoverished noble is followed by a one-time event: once he found no servant and himself ran before him for three mil.
Rav Nahman's arrival in Sura only frames a halakhic question-and-answer exchange; standard rabbinic dialogue with no conflict or change.
Rabba reports finding scholars discussing a dispute and what he told them; purely scholarly speech with no event.
A report of Rav Huna's habitual practice when litigants came before him; nothing follows from it.
Rav Ashi puts food in Mar Zutra's mouth, is challenged by the butler and soldiers, they check the meat and find leprosy: multiple actions, conflict and resolution.
A bandit taken to execution confesses to a killing, and on that basis the victim's wife is married off; an incident with actions and a change, followed by legal debate over its meaning.
Rav Amram, tempted by a captive woman, lifts the ladder, stops halfway, cries fire, is shamed by the Sages and exorcises his evil inclination: a full narrative with conflict and change.
Rav Hisda praises Rav Hamnuna, Rav Huna summons him, sees he wears no head-cloth, turns his face away and bans him until he marries: actions, conflict and a change.
Hypothetical legal analogies and objections about consecrating a mortgaged field; no narrated event.
A report of what was sung when Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi were ordained; a single act with no continuation or change.
Ravina comes before Rav Ashi with a question and receives a ruling; as in Ketubot 50b, coming before a rabbi and being ruled on, with no further narrated action or change, is not a story.

A couple comes before Rav Nahman, who recognizes the woman's accent and rules, is challenged and reverses his ruling; mostly speech around a ruling, with a slight action (hearing her voice) and a change of ruling.

An incident in Shihin: an inherited mustard branch breaks, yields nine kav, and its wood roofs a booth; a narrated wonder with several actions, the kind of eyewitness wonder he accepted in review (open edge of R-C5).
A man makes a conditional divorce, arrives on time but is blocked by the ferry, cries out, and Shmuel rules the divorce valid: an incident with actions and a change followed by a ruling.
Only reports Rabbi Zeira's habitual avoidance of Rav Yehuda, then turns to Rav Yehuda's dictum; no event follows within the passage.
A Jerusalem family whose members die young consults Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, follows his advice to study Torah, lives, and is renamed after him: actions and a change.

Dying Mar Ukva asks for his charity records, finds the sum inadequate, and gives away half his wealth: actions and change. The Gemara's ensuing legal question is commentary (R-B4), within the same segment.
Part of the Dosa ben Harkinas episode: the Sages enter and leave by three doors, Rabbi Akiva is encountered, challenged, withstands it and is mocked; actions with conflict.
A man comes before Rabbi Ami with testimony, is questioned, and Rabbi Ami rules; like Ketubot 50b, a coming-before-a-rabbi and ruling with no other narrated action or change.
A witness recounts the traveler who drove off a troop with a fig branch and later died; Rabbi Tarfon cross-examines him and permits the wife to remarry: a full incident with actions and a change.
A debtor sells two plots, the creditor repossesses one and comes for the other, and the buyer brings a hundred dinars to buy him off: a 'certain man' incident with several actions.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya hears of a captive child in Rome, tests him with a verse, vows to ransom him, does so, and the child becomes Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha: a full narrative with change.
Levi expounds twice and the audience's reaction changes; the events are teaching (speech) with a response, enough change to be borderline but not a full narrative.
A brother arrives, demands a share, is rebuffed, comes before Rav Hisda who reverses the burden of proof against a violent man: an incident with actions, conflict and resolution.
A brief recollection of a halitza and Rabbi Tarfon's instruction, cited as evidence of practice; nothing follows and there is no change.
Rav Huna found the Sages discussing and disagreed with them; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no event or conflict beyond debate.
A habitual frame followed by a one-time event: Rav Rehumi fails to come home, his wife weeps, the roof collapses and he dies.
A son questions his father's ruling and is told to be silent; standard rabbinic dialogue with no action beyond speech.
Two sages stand for Rabbi Shimon bar Abba and he objects; a small incident carried mainly by speech with only mild conflict and no real change.
A rebellious wife is compelled by Mar Zutra and from the couple R. Hanina of Sura is born: incident, ruling and a consequence.
R. Ya'akov ben Dostai's eyewitness account of walking ankle-deep in fig honey is the one-line eyewitness wonder the expert accepted for Ketubot 111b; the other 'I saw' sizes are bare descriptions.
Dicta plus Rabbi Elazar seeing a field and remarking on it; speech without conflict or anything following.
The Sages award an allowance and Nakdimon's daughter answers with a barbed blessing they answer amen to; beyond the ruling the only action is speech, though with conflict.
The Sages sought to permit the Gibeonites and Rabbi objected; a legal deliberation in speech with no narrated event or change.
A full story about Nebuzaradan and the blood of Zechariah, biblical-era figures; the expert ruled this very passage out of scope.
A man betroths with a myrtle mat, is challenged, redirects to the coins inside, the woman takes it and stays silent, and Rava rules: an incident with several actions plus a ruling.
Within the sages' frame are two narrated incidents: the captive betrothed couple who never touched until his death, and the grain price that fell until sinners were found and stoned.
R. Yehuda bars Meir's students, Sumakhos pushes in, R. Yehuda grows angry and R. Yosei responds: actions, emotion and conflict.
A yevama falls to a man and his brother wants to disqualify her, but the passage narrates only their negotiation; speech with conflict and no further event in the span.
Descriptions of Judean wedding customs with no one-time event following.
A Jew and a gentile walk together, the gentile tries to slow him by reminding him of the Temple, he sighs yet keeps pace, and they exchange words: actions, conflict and a turn.
Residents dig a diversion channel, upstream owners complain to Abaye, and he orders the diversion removed: an incident with actions besides the ruling.
Rav Yehuda's summons before Rav Nahman, the litigant's Hasmonean claim, Rav Mattana's arrival, the torn marriage contracts and the attempted stoning form an extended narrative.
A one-line eyewitness report of an Arab cutting open his camel, cited as evidence; the open eyewitness-wonder category between a bare report and a story.
At his son's wedding Rava pours drinks, some sages stand and others do not, and he becomes angry: actions, an emotional reaction and conflict.
A man passes bareheaded and Ravina and R. Yirmeya comment; a small incident carried mainly by speech with little conflict or change.
A man rents out a millstone, grows rich, buys his own and demands cash, and the renter refuses: an incident with change and conflict; Ravina's and Rav Avira's analysis is commentary.
Two narrated incidents (a man rode a horse on Shabbat; a man cohabited under a fig tree), each followed by the court's action of stoning or flogging. Incident plus response fits R-C0.
Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai meets the impoverished daughter of Nakdimon. There is a sequence of actions, an encounter, a reversal of fortune and his weeping, so this is a full narrative.
Post-biblical captive children deliberate and then leap into the sea, the girls first and then the boys. These are multiple actions with a change, and they are in scope.
A court case made of litigants' requests, a judge's instruction and a colleague's retort. It is almost entirely speech, with some conflict but no further narrated action beyond the ruling.
Rav Aha arrives, takes his great-granddaughter onto his lap, and Rav Hisda challenges the act. A narrated action draws a response, though most of what follows is halakhic exchange.
Scholars meet, pose a contradiction, fall silent and take it to Rabba, who answers. This is standard rabbinic dialogue with no event beyond the speech and no conflict beyond ordinary challenge.

A man brings the first shearing, and R. Yishmael refuses it, recuses himself and seats other judges. He then observes his own bias as he comes and goes. There are several actions and an internal change.
Rav Hisda's slave escapes to the Samaritans, and a contentious exchange of messages follows over his return. Segment 3 is the Gemara's commentary on the story and is excluded under R-B4.
A woman holding deposited documents is sued by the heirs, claims she seized them, and Rav Nahman rules against her. This is an incident with actions and a dispute, followed by a ruling.
A habitual frame, the weekly return marked by a pillar of fire, leads to a one-time event: he is delayed, R. Yannai's word misfires, and Yehuda dies.
The sons buy a maidservant and leave silver as collateral. Her price rises, the sellers want to cancel, and Rabbi Ami rules. This is an incident with change, followed by a ruling.
A hypothetical legal case from a baraita ('if one's bread was baked...'), not a narrated event.
Purely halakhic analysis of the Mishna's rulings. Nothing is narrated.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives come to him with a costly medical situation, he advises them, and he later regrets it. The regret is an emotional reaction and a change, so this is more than a ruling.
Judges rule, Reish Lakish reverses them and R. Yohanan rebukes him. There is an action and a reversal, but the incident itself is barely given, and the rebuke is ordinary scholarly criticism.
A brewer betroths a woman with someone else's sediment, the owner finds him and comments, and Rava rules. This is an incident with several actions, then a ruling.
A man enters the synagogue, takes a Torah scroll and gives it to his wife as a divorce, and Rav Yosef rules. A narrated incident with multiple actions, then a ruling.
A transmission frame: R. Zeira found R. Asi teaching a ruling. Only speech, with no event or conflict.
A widow seizes a silver cup toward her ketubah, demands sustenance, and Rava rules for her. A seizure and a claim are narrated before the ruling, though the story is thin.
The event is a verbal exchange about betrothal followed by a ruling. There is no narrated action beyond the speech and no conflict.
A millstone is rented for grinding, then the owner becomes rich and buys his own mill and donkey, and a dispute arises. There are multiple actions and a change.
A husband travels, spends 600 to retrieve his wife's 400 and takes one dinar on the way back, then comes before R. Ami, whose ruling is challenged and revised. Actions and a change.
During a drought everyone sells their mansions, then wheat arrives, and Rav Nahman rules that the sales are void. Events and a change, followed by a ruling.
A bare report that Rabbi once gave an orphan one-twelfth, cited as evidence inside halakhic argument. Nothing else is narrated.
An exchange of halakhic letters between two Tannaim. It is pure speech, and the sharp tone is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, not conflict.
Bar Kappara sits in a bathhouse, fails to rise for R. Shimon, who becomes angry and complains to his father, who responds; several actions, an emotional reaction and a resolution.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi tricks the Angel of Death, leaps into paradise, keeps the knife until a Divine Voice intervenes, and meets R. Shimon ben Yohai; a full narrative with many actions and change.
Rav Pappa serves drinks at his son's wedding, Rav Yitzhak fails to stand, and Rav Pappa becomes angry; narrated actions plus an emotional reaction count as an event.
Rav Yosef son of Rava leaves his studies to go home, his father takes a weapon and confronts him, and both miss the pre-fast meal; multiple actions, conflict and consequence.
Ravina finding Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak pondering is only a frame for an unresolved halakhic dilemma; nothing happens beyond the question.
Rav Nahman arrives in Sura and is asked a legal question which he answers; ordinary scholarly exchange with no event or change beyond speech.
Two incidents: a bathhouse and a staircase collapse under R. Abbahu and R. Yohanan, who pull up their supporters, followed by a challenge and reply; actions and change.

The sharecropper's habitual gift breaks pattern one day, R. Yishmael refuses it and recuses himself, appoints judges, and then finds himself biased; a one-time event after a custom with several actions and an inner change.
A man deposits silk with Rav Dimi, who dies without instructions, and the claimant comes before R. Abba who rules; a narrated incident with more than one action followed by a ruling.
Legal discussion and a hypothetical baraita case ('if one's bread was baked...'); no event that happened is narrated.
The incident of a debtor who hid his money with a gentile and was forced to sell is only alluded to in a sentence to explain a ruling, not narrated in full.
Giddel bar Re'ilai pays taxes in advance, the owners return and reclaim the land, and the case goes before Rav Pappa who is corrected by Rav Huna; several actions, conflict and resolution.
Someone comes before Rav Yosef, who rules, followed by scholarly back-and-forth with Abaye; like the orphan daughters of 50b there is no other narrated action or change besides the ruling.

First-person eyewitness wonders (walking ankle-deep in fig honey, seeing the land flowing with milk and honey); the rule register notes he accepted the Ketubot 111b eyewitness wonder in review and lists it in 2005.
A man brings R. Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing, is questioned, R. Yishmael refuses it and recuses himself, appoints judges, and discovers his own bias; several actions and an inner change.
A single act (betrothing a minor with vegetables in the market) cited as the basis for Ravina's ruling, with no further action or change.
A rumor of betrothal, Rav Hama summons the father, who explains the conditional betrothal and the groom's violating journey, and Rav Hama rules; an incident with several actions followed by a ruling.
A man testifies before Reish Lakish and the passage is a legal exchange and challenge from R. Elazar; standard rabbinic dialogue without an event beyond speech.

Brief wonder reports (a mustard branch breaks yielding nine kav, its wood roofs a booth; a giant cabbage stalk) cited as evidence of fertility; close to the open eyewitness-wonder case, with minimal action and change.
A bare report of how many wedding blessings Levi and Rav Asi recited, cited as evidence of practice; nothing follows.
After R. Eliezer's death four sages enter to refute him and R. Yehoshua rebukes them; almost entirely speech, with some conflict in the posthumous challenge and rebuke.
A report of how Ravina allocated the dowry, cited as legal proof; no incident with action or change is narrated.
Rav Hisda's habitual response to complainants plus Gemara discussion; a custom with no one-time event following.
An incident only mentioned ('I was involved in an incident') as precedent for a ruling; none of it is narrated.
The incident of ten men carrying a woman out on a bier is only alluded to in one line as evidence, its details left to be filled in, like the widow incident on the same page.

Ze'eiri avoids R. Yohanan, carries him across a puddle, and is confronted about refusing his daughter: several actions with conflict. The Gemara's closing comment in [3] is commentary (R-B4) but sits inside the segment.
The incident of Me'oret making her slave perform three acts so that he died is only alluded to as an objection. It is barely narrated, which fits R-C6's alluded incident.

Rav Nahman's relative sells her ketubah, is divorced and dies, the buyers sue, Rav Nahman gives advice, the daughter acts on it, and he regrets it. That is multiple actions with change. The Gemara's explanation in [4] is commentary.
A man wills a palm tree to his daughter and the orphans divide the estate without giving it, followed by rulings. This is an incident with actions followed by a ruling (R-C0's cow shape).
R. Yirmeya dozes, wakes and rebukes the two Sages as 'children'. Apart from dozing and waking it is scholarly dialogue with a rebuke, which is close to the standard discourse Jeff excluded.
Abaye's boast and a Sage's challenge lead into a purely halakhic exchange. This is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no event (R-C2, 21b ruling).
The passage is only the opening statement of a fact (Rami bar Hama's sister was married to Rav Avya). The events of the story lie in the following context, not in the passage.
A court exchange: a woman owes an oath, the opposing litigant and she make requests, and the judge rules. It is almost entirely speech-acts, with litigant conflict but no other narrated action.
Shmuel is crossing on a ferry, a man helps him, and Shmuel recuses himself from the man's case. There are actions with a consequence.
Terminological discussion and Rabbi Hiyya's teachings. No narrated event.
Only halakhic reasoning plus two bare reports of men called 'son of an Aramean' and a rabbi's ruling. No further narrated action or change (R-C0 limit, 50b).
Mar Zutra visits the dying convert, sees his condition worsen, and acquires the slave by having him carry his shoes: actions and change. Segments [3]-[4] are the Gemara's commentary.
R. Yohanan's relatives seize the orphans' cow and go back and forth between R. Yohanan and Reish Lakish, with conflicting rulings. This is an incident with action and conflict.
A question about a bill of divorce is sent and answered: quasi-speech-acts with no conflict and no narrated event beyond the ruling.
Rav Ami's permission, the Sages' objection and his reply are mostly speech-acts with conflict and implied change. This is the Ketubot 7a case Jeff ruled borderline.
Two linked testimony incidents. The second ends with Reish Lakish looking harshly at R. Elazar and rebuking him: an action, conflict and a realization beyond ordinary dialogue.
Rava goes to meet a man passing in a gilt carriage, Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak refuses until he recognizes him, then goes too. Rav Nahman bar Yaakov uncovers his arm; several actions and a change.
A baraita deriving the dates of Moses' death and birth from verses. This is exegesis, not narration, and in any case concerns a biblical figure.
Analytical discussion of why Abaye and Rava chose their sources. No narrated event.
A hypothetical case about a general arriving in a city, analyzed legally. It is not an event that happened (R-C0 hypothetical).

Marta bat Baitos brings a measure of dinars to King Yannai until he appoints Yehoshua ben Gamla High Priest: two actions and a change. These are post-biblical figures, and the Gemara's citation of the Mishnah incident is includable.
A creditor seizes an ox from the orphans' herdsman, they dispute, and they come before Rav Nahman for a ruling. This is the incident-plus-ruling shape with a narrated action (seizure).
A narrated history: men would not marry, successive ordinances, husbands still divorced in anger, until Shimon ben Shatah enacted a reform. Habitual conduct leading to change (R-C3, 61a).
Peleimu's daily habit is followed by a one-time event: Satan appears as a pauper on Yom Kippur eve and is brought in and fed. This is a habitual frame followed by narrated actions.
The passage is only the opening words 'a certain man was selling'. The incident itself lies in the following context, so the passage holds no story on its own.
Mostly a halakhic query sent and answered (quasi-speech acts); Rav Huna's death in the interim is the only event, so it sits on the borderline rather than a full story.
Homa comes before Rava, her arm is exposed, Rava goes home, and his wife drives Homa out of Mehoza: multiple actions, conflict and change.
Rabbis consider a ruling and are rebuked by a colleague; ordinary scholarly exchange with no narrated event beyond speech.
A hypothetical legal dilemma posed, researched and answered by letter; speech and quasi-speech acts with no conflict or narrated incident.
Rabbi Akiva sees a ship sink, grieves for Rabbi Meir, then meets him alive in Cappadocia and hears how he was saved: a narrated event with change.
A man brings Rav Anan a gift, Rav Anan disqualifies himself and sends him to Rav Nahman, who gives him precedence, and the opponent loses: a chain of actions with consequences.
Mishnah and legal-exegetical discussion; the Rebecca verse is analyzed for its language, not narrated.
A maidservant immerses, a bone is found in her teeth, and Rabbi orders another immersion: an incident with more than one action followed by a ruling.
A man sells his mother's ketubah rights, she dies, he contests the sale, and the rabbis rule: the incident-plus-ruling shape with several actions and a change.
Pure legal argument about hypothetical consecrations; nothing happened.
Rabbi Hananya leaves for twelve years, returns, finds his daughter, his wife dies of shock and is revived by his prayer: a full narrative.
A virginity dispute brought to Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi, who tests maidservants and then the bride and rules: multiple actions resolving a conflict.
Court episodes in Rava's court: the oath is reversed on his wife's word, and Rav Pappa's testimony is refused. The episodes are mostly speech, with only a thin narrated change.
A woman asks a bead seller for a string and gives a mocking answer to his betrothal offer, followed by a ruling. It is almost entirely speech, with a slight conflict and no other action or change.
A bare report of a betrothal with rags and its valuation, cited as precedent; nothing follows.
Post-biblical narrative of the Roman abuse of captive Jewish children and the Beitar schoolchildren who fought and were burned: actions and change. The opening verse exegesis is not part of it.
A father bequeaths a palm tree, the orphans divide the estate without giving it, and the rabbis rule: incident with conflict and ruling.
The letter embeds an incident of a man who longed to leave the Land for a woman, heard this teaching, and stayed suffering until his death: actions and change. The rest is advice.
The incident is only mentioned as coming before Rabbi Yitzhak and none of it is narrated. What follows is a legal statement.
A claimed brother comes demanding an inheritance, is rebuffed, and goes to Rav Hisda, who shifts the burden of proof onto the violent man: real conflict, actions and a ruling.
A man removes a feather from Ameimar's head (or covers spittle for Mar Ukva) and the judge disqualifies himself. Each incident has an action that leads to a change.
A debtor dies, the creditor seizes the land, the orphans pay, the creditor seizes it again, and Abaye rules: several actions and a ruling.
A poor man shares Rabbi Nehemya's lentils and dies, and Rabbi Nehemya laments: actions with a drastic change. The Gemara's gloss on his words is minor.
Rav Yosef bar Hama collects Rav Sheshet's money, is asked to make an acquisition, evades it, and is praised: a sequence of actions with an outcome.
Someone comes before Rav Yosef, he rules, and Abaye challenges him: per Jeff's 50b ruling, coming before a rabbi and being ruled on, plus scholarly dialogue, is not a story.
The brothers divided their property (a narrated action) and came before Rav Ashi, who ruled: an incident followed by a ruling.
A chain of narrated events: Hanina declines the appointment, Afes presides, Afes dies, Hanina takes his place, Levi moves to Babylonia, and Rav infers this from a report.
The relatives come with a real problem, Rabbi Yohanan advises them, and he later regrets it, which is a change.
An incident only alluded to as evidence; the details have to be filled in from commentary, so R-C6 makes it borderline.
The husband dies, the orphans spread the robe over his corpse, the widow claims it, and Rava rules: an incident with actions followed by a ruling.
A betrothal with a stone, Rav Hisda's appraisal, and the mother's challenge and his reply give an incident with several actions and a ruling.
These are reports of statements and habitual practices about orla, with no incident, conflict or change.
The men borrow, cannot repay and are seized as slaves, then come before Rav Huna, who rules after being challenged: an incident with actions followed by a ruling.
A man states where he comes from and a rabbi identifies the place; this is speech used as a springboard for a lineage discussion, with no conflict or change.
The husband takes a second wife and gives her a maidservant, the first wife cries out before Rava, and he ignores her: several actions and conflict.
Two incidents: a bathhouse and a stair collapse, and in each the rabbi climbs out pulling his helpers up, followed by a dialogue explaining why.
A debt is paid through an agent, the creditors refuse to return the document, and the case comes before Rabbi Abbahu for a ruling: an incident with conflict.
A habitual frame, Tarfon's care for his mother, leads to a one-time event: he boasts in the study hall and is rebuked.
A man contests a field and dies, the steward argues the orphans' case before Abaye over several turns and wins, and Abaye praises him.
One ruling (a permission to marry) followed by standard scholarly back-and-forth about sources; nothing further happens.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba questions the woman and tricks the yavam into halitza and then a proper halitza: actions, conflict and change.
Cited as proof: Rav Yehuda repeatedly extracts a divorce, the husband voids it, and the witnesses stop their ears and write it against his will. Several actions and conflict.
A man sells his property, goes up to the Land, fails to settle and seeks to undo the sale, and Rava rules: an incident with actions followed by a ruling.
Rabbi Elazar refutes Rabbi Yohanan, who falls silent, praises him, learns the source is a baraita, and goes out to master Torat Kohanim: actions and change.
Apart from the sages' allocation there is only speech: her ironic blessing and their amen. Some implied tension, but no further action.
The reservoir is measured and found deficient, Tarfon and Akiva dispute the case, and Tarfon finally concedes and praises Akiva: an incident with a resolution and change.
Rabbi Zeira finds no ferry and crosses by a rope, a Sadducee mocks him, and he answers: actions plus conflict.
A bare report that two rabbis each made a ruling, with no narrated incident or consequence.
A one-line eyewitness wonder: he arrives, sees the goats, figs and mixing liquids, and responds. This is the shape the expert has accepted (Ketubot 111b).
A man deposits a goblet, the depositary dies without instructions, and the claimants come before Rav Nahman, who rules: an incident with actions followed by a ruling.
A halakhic question asked and answered, overheard by Rabbi Abbahu; speech only with no conflict and no event beyond the exchange.
A report of Rav Aha's habitual practice followed by a question and answer; the habit leads to no change and the dialogue is ordinary, without conflict.
A narrated incident with a ruling, but beyond entering the shop it is almost entirely a speech exchange; the woman's mocking reply gives some conflict, making it borderline.
Purely legal argumentation about konamot and liens; no event is narrated.
King Agrippa, a post-biblical figure, rerouted his entourage before a bride and the Sages responded by praising him: an event with a response, embedded after a baraita ruling.
Abaye's tenant asks, Abaye rules, Rav Yosef corrects him, and Abaye runs three parasangs after the tenant but fails to catch him, then draws the lesson; multiple actions and a change.

A betrothed couple come before Rava, who places an intermediary between them because he sees they are familiar with each other; an incident with an action and observation beyond the bare ruling, told in two versions.
The opening of the incident of Rabban Gamliel and the Elders traveling on a ship, which the Talmud quotes from the Mishnah; a narrated event involving rabbis.
Continuation of the Yeimar bar Hashu boat story: the rabbis seize the boat, dispute ownership, are challenged by Rav Pinehas, and are rebuked by Rava; multiple actions and conflict.
The blind man is late, Mar Shmuel sends a messenger, the messenger reports adultery, and Shmuel rules: a sequence of events. Segment 3 is the Gemara's interpretive commentary and is excluded.
A man wills a palm tree to his daughter; the orphans divide the estate and withhold it; the rabbis rule: an incident with actions followed by a ruling, like the stolen-cow case.
Yeimar bar Hashu sends his agent to seize a boat, the agent does so, and two rabbis encounter and challenge him: several actions and conflict, the start of a longer story.

Continuation of Reish Lakish's condolence visit, in which he has his disseminator deliver a series of blessings to the mourners; segment 4 is Abaye's halakhic commentary on the wording and is not part of the story.
Two incidents: Mar bar Rav Ashi surgically trims a man's member and declares him fit, and Rav Pappi sharply rebukes Rav Beivai's lenient ruling; events with actions and a response.
Two deeds come before Rav Yosef, who rules, and the losing party argues; coming before a rabbi and being ruled on, with no other narrated action or change, is not enough.
Abaye accuses Rav Ika of self-interest, and they go and ask Rav Hananel; mostly speech and quasi-speech acts, but the accusation is real conflict beyond ordinary debate.
Cases of a man coming before Rav Yehuda and Rava and receiving a ruling; no narrated action or change beyond the ruling.
The tail of a dialogue, a halakhic conclusion, and a one-line allusion to a woman who strangled her child, cited as evidence and dismissed; it is a single act with no further development.
A woman comes before Rav Nahman and argues him into compelling a divorce; it is all speech, but her challenge is conflict and implies a change in the ruling.

Rav Hiyya Arikha supports his widowed sister-in-law for 25 years, refuses her claims, is sued, ignores the ruling, has his property seized, and appeals to Rava, who argues with her: many actions, conflict and change.
A brief citation that Beit Hillel ruled Queen Helene must be a nazirite seven more years; as given in the text it is a single ruling cited as proof, with the incident only alluded to.
The ending of the story of the man who kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot (he forced the sons to support their father); the rest of the segment is the Gemara's commentary and is not part of the story.

Continuation of the story of Marta bat Baitos during the siege of Jerusalem: her death, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's response, and her casting away her gold; post-biblical figures with multiple actions.
A scholarly exchange between Abaye and Rav Dimi: an objection, a silence, a suggested answer and praise. This is standard rabbinic dialogue without conflict or a narrated event.
A man passes without covering his head and Ravina remarks on his rudeness, to which Rabbi Yirmeya replies; there is a small narrated event, but the response is only speech with mild conflict.
Baraita halakha and Gemara analysis of hypothetical cases; no narrated event.
Avimi sends money via Hama, who pays, demands the document and is refused; the dispute comes before R. Abbahu who rules. Several actions plus conflict and resolution.
Reports of R. Yohanan's and Rava's habitual practice cited as evidence for a halakha; nothing follows from the habit.
A bare report of Rav Zevid's ruling or practice, with no response or change.
Abaye rules for his tenant, learns from Rav Yosef that the ruling was wrong, and runs after the tenant without catching him. Several actions and a change.
The widow bakes the dinar into bread, swears falsely without knowing it, and her child dies. Segment 4 is the Gemara's commentary, so it is not part of the story.
Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebels and seizes a garment, and the sages rule. Rav Gamda accuses them of flattery: an incident with actions, a ruling and conflict.
Mostly speech: a report of what happened in the study hall. Reish Lakish screaming and being ignored gives it conflict, but little action.
Two bare reports, Rav Kahana taking a cloth and Mar bar Rav Ashi buying one, cited as precedents with no continuation.

A frame narrative of inquiry leads to the incident: the dying master throws his hat to the crying maidservant to free her, and Rav Nahman rules. Segment 5 is the Gemara's commentary, and segment 2 is dicta.
A man makes a conditional divorce, returns, is stopped by the ferry and calls out, and Shmuel rules. A narrated incident with several actions, followed by a ruling.
Largely dialogue between Geneiva and Rav Huna and Rav Hisda, with some implied tension ("an argumentative person") and minimal action: he approaches, is offered food, declines.
The maidservant is captured and redeemed by a gentile as his wife, and the sages send instructions to her master. Several events and a resolution.
Abba bar Marta owes money, disguises his forehead with wax and passes his creditors unrecognized. Several actions with an outcome.
A one-line report that Rava coerced Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity, cited as precedent with no narrative development.
Ravin the Pious goes to betroth a woman for his son and betroths her to himself instead. Two actions and a change; the Gemara's justification that follows is commentary.
The relatives consult R. Yohanan, then Reish Lakish, who threatens them, and return to R. Yohanan, who yields. Several actions and clear conflict.
Rabbis redeem captives, one is found pregnant by a gentile, and they come before R. Ami for a ruling. Rav Yosef's later reaction is halakhic discussion rather than part of the story.
The Gemara quotes the Mishnah incident of the divorce document brought before Rabban Gamliel in Kfar Otnai. Jeff named Gittin 10b's citation as includable.
A scribe comes before R. Abbahu with a question and receives a ruling. Beyond that there is no other narrated action or change (the limit of R-C0, as in Ketubot 50b).
Brothers negotiate over the yevama and the property, with conflict and distrust, but the passage is almost entirely speech.
Halakhic discussion. The incident of the woman who strangled her child is only mentioned as a single act cited as evidence, with no narration.
Only an opening fragment ("a certain person said to them"), with no narrated event within the passage.
Scholarly maneuvering: the sages reverse the names and send the question to Rav, who swears. These are mostly quasi-speech acts, with some implied conflict and irony.
The convert's son and Rav Beivai quarrel over a city office and come before Rav Yosef; Rav Adda bar Ahava intervenes and the offices are divided. Conflict, actions and a change.
Rabba reports finding scholars discussing a dispute and his reply; ordinary scholarly dialogue with no narrated action or change.
A woman comes before Rabbi Ami and an argued exchange makes him reverse his ruling; almost entirely speech, but with real conflict and an implied change.
A man bequeaths a palm tree, dies and leaves only two halves: an incident that actually happened, with more than one action and a change, which then goes for a ruling.
A legal dilemma and an interpretation; Rav Yosef's sharp retort is standard rabbinic back-and-forth, not a story.
The will, the death leaving two half-trees, and Rav Ashi's deliberation and the ruling form an incident followed by its resolution.
A bare report that Rabba ruled on a found bill of divorce; the incident is barely narrated, and the details are disputed as variant traditions.
A report of what Rav Kahana did with the orphan's beer, cited with his rationale as precedent; nothing follows from it.
At his son's wedding Rav Pappa pours a cup, the guest fails to stand, and Rav Pappa becomes angry: actions plus an emotional reaction, which counts as an event.
Two incidents: a man removes a feather or covers spittle, is questioned, and the judge disqualifies himself. Actions lead to a change.
A man comes before the rabbis, they rule, and a colleague challenges them from a baraita; coming before rabbis and being ruled on, with scholarly dispute, is not enough (R-C0's limit).
Pearls are deposited, the custodian dies without instructions, the parties come before Rabbi Ami and he rules: several narrated actions and a change, then a ruling.
The judges report that Rav Yehuda ruled in a case of branches; the incident is only alluded to and is cited as precedent.
A full narrative: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha's captive children are paired by their masters, recognize each other at dawn and die weeping. They are post-biblical figures, so in scope.
During a famine the Sages ask Rav Yosef to pray and he refuses with an argument; mainly speech, with some tension, but no further action is narrated.
Rav Hisda and Rav Yosef exchange legal reasoning, in two versions; standard rabbinic dialogue with no event.
A man appoints agents in the synagogue and the schoolteacher then dies, prompting a dispute and a ruling: an incident with actions and a change, followed by its resolution.
A hypothetical legal case from a baraita (if a parent dies before the wedding), not an event that happened.
Aher sees Hutzpit's tongue dragged, reacts, and goes out and sins: an event that leads to a change in a post-biblical figure.
A debtor sells two plots, the creditor seizes one and comes for the other, and the buyer offers him the money: several actions and a conflict.
After Shmuel and Karna disagree, the Sages swap the names, send the question to Rav, and he swears in Shmuel's favour: a narrated action with conflict and a result.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seize the orphans' cow, go back and forth between Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish, and are told to return it: several actions, conflict and change.
Ulla's remark shames Rav Hamnuna (an emotional reaction counts as an event), and a further exchange clears his lineage: conflict and a change, beyond ordinary dialogue.
One rabbi praises a ruling and another rebukes him; Jeff ruled that this is ordinary Talmudic dialogue, not a story.
Rabban Gamliel sees Rabbi Akiva's ship sink, grieves, then meets him alive and hears how he survived: a full narrated incident with a change.
A man snatches a belt from a woman and offers it back as betrothal; she takes it in silence, and Rav Nahman rules on it. Actions and conflict, then a ruling.
A man and bride come before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi, who has the cloth brought, washes it and finds blood, then rules: several narrated actions and a resolution.
A man testifies before R. Yehoshua ben Levi, who questions him and then elevates the other man to Levite status; the elevation is an action that changes his status. Close to the R-C0 limit, though.
A man sells his mother's ketubah rights, his mother dies, he contests the sale, and Rami bar Hama and Rava rule: an incident with several actions, followed by a ruling.
Two short incidents of a woman's mocking reply to a betrothal offer, ruled on by Rav Hama; almost entirely speech, with no further action or change, but the mockery is conflict.
A man snatches a belt from a woman selling belts, proposes betrothal, and she takes it back in silence; Rav Nahman rules. An incident with actions, followed by a ruling.
A Mishnah legal case stated in general terms (one who marries a woman...), with no narrated event.
A dispute over transmission: questions sent and an attribution recalled. Only speech and quasi-speech acts, with no conflict beyond ordinary scholarly discourse.
Rav Ashi's slave Minyamin is immersed by Ravina and Rav Aha with a bridle and a clay bucket; several narrated actions. Segments 4-5 are a separate halakhic question.

At his son's wedding Rabban Gamliel serves the rabbis drinks; one refuses the cup, another accepts it, and they dispute it. The Abraham exemplum is cited inside a rabbinic story, so it stays in scope.
R. Elazar reports a teaching and Shmuel mocks it; later R. Zeira hears it recited. This is teaching and a sharp retort, which counts as ordinary rabbinic dialogue rather than story conflict.
The bar Tzartzur heirs come before Rav Amram, ignore his advice, are threatened with excommunication and sent to Rav Nahman: actions, conflict and a ruling.
Rav Hiyya bar Adda is absent three days harvesting a miraculous vine and is rebuked by Reish Lakish: narrated events with a consequence.
Something happens to someone (Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna loses the study hall keys on Shabbat) and a rabbi responds (R. Pedat tells him what to do). The Gemara's inference in segment 3 is commentary.
An incident that came before R. Yitzhak in Antioch is only mentioned, with no content narrated; only the ruling is given.
A man sells his property to go to Eretz Yisrael, goes, fails to settle, and Rava rules on it: several actions and a change.
Mishnah story: a girl goes to draw water, is raped, and R. Yohanan ben Nuri rules. A narrated incident, but it belongs to the Mishnah under R-C1.
Shmuel's father guards captive women; later Shmuel's own daughters are taken captive, outmanoeuvre their captors in R. Hanina's court and are permitted: a full narrative with a reversal.
A hypothetical case the Gemara constructs (we elevated him, we downgraded him), not an event that happened.
Embedded in Rav Ulla's answer: the Sages seek a deal with Dama ben Netina, who forgoes the profit rather than wake his father. A post-biblical figure, so in scope.
Rav Pappa goes to have a ketubah written; Yehuda bar Mareimar comes out to meet him and takes his leave at the door: narrated actions leading into an exchange.
A woman comes before Rav Nehemya and asks for sustenance and wine, which he grants. That is coming before a rabbi and being ruled on, with no other narrated action or change (the R-C0 limit).
The dying Mar Ukva reviews his charity records and gives away half his wealth: actions and a change. The Gemara's halakhic question after it is commentary.
R. Yehuda from India falls ill; Mar Zutra visits and acquires his slave as he dies: several actions and a change.
A man brings Rav Anan a gift; Rav Anan disqualifies himself, accepts the gift, and sends him to Rav Nahman, who misreads the letter: actions, conflict and consequences.
R. Zeira crosses the Jordan on a rope bridge and is challenged by a Sadducee, whom he answers: an action plus a conflict.
An incident happened (Beloreya's slaves preempted her and immersed first), came before the Sages, and they ruled the slaves became free: an action plus a change and a ruling.

Letters sent, a rabbi goes as messenger under threat of excommunication, the offended Rav Anan goes to Mar Ukva: several actions and sharp interpersonal conflict, well beyond ordinary scholarly back-and-forth.
Parents quarrel over the match, the wife forces the father to agree, and during the meal his relative climbs to the roof and betroths the girl: several actions, conflict and a change.

Shmuel's father guards the captives, Shmuel's daughters are captured, outwit their captors in R. Hanina's court and are permitted, and R. Hanina tells Rav Shemen to marry one: a full narrative with irony and change.
A baraita describing a general custom and halakhot about wedding days; no particular event is narrated.

A courtroom exchange: a litigant's request, the woman's demand, a judge's order and a colleague's insult. It is almost all speech, with no narrated change beyond the ruling, though there is real conflict.
A mother deeds her property to two sons on the same day, each goes to a different judge and wins, and the judges confront each other: several actions and conflict.
The teacher is absent three days, harvests a miraculous vine with dwindling yield, and Reish Lakish ties the dwindling to his absence: events, causality and change.
Courts rule and collect for daughters, and Rav Nahman threatens to seize the judges' houses unless they reverse. That is conflict, but it is told as rulings and a threat with no narrated outcome.
Rav Hisda tells Rabba to look into a halakha and he does. This is study and teaching, with no conflict or change.
A question put to R. Eliezer and his answer, followed by the Gemara's inference: a speech-act with no conflict.
A debtor dies, the creditor seizes the land, the orphans pay to redeem it, he seizes it again and they go to Abaye, who rules: several actions and a ruling, the R-C0 cow-case shape.
The Gemara's commentary on the Mishnah's innkeeper story, explaining and supplementing its details; per R-B4 not itself a story.
Three sisters' sons die after circumcision and the fourth sister comes before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who rules: narrated events with causality, followed by a ruling.
A bare report that Rav Kahana took a cloth for a redemption and valued it at five sela, cited as a precedent. Nothing follows and there is no change.

An agent cannot find the intermediary, three Sages offer to take the agency, Rav Safra objects and they are embarrassed: actions, conflict and an emotional change. Segments 4-5 are later Amoraic commentary (R-B4).
Rav Huna's habitual practice of asking litigants for a water-drawer is a custom cited as evidence; no one-time event follows.
Purely halakhic discussion of the opinions of Rav and Shmuel; no narrated event.
Only notes where the Mishnah's incident took place, as part of the legal argument; it narrates nothing.
From a habit comes a one-time event: Rav Rehumi stays away, his wife weeps, and the roof collapses and he dies. Clear actions, emotion and causal change.
From a habit comes a one-time event: Rav Rehumi stays away, his wife weeps, and the roof collapses and he dies. Clear actions, emotion and causal change.
One act (betrothal with silk) cited as the occasion for an Amoraic dispute and its analysis; no further action or change is narrated.

R. Hama returns after twelve years, meets his son without recognising him, is distressed, then stands before him at home and his wife reveals who the son is: actions, emotion and a recognition. Rami bar Hama's verse is commentary.
Homa comes before Rava and her arm is exposed, Rava goes home aroused, and his wife beats Homa out of Mehoza: several actions, conflict and change.
Abaye's habit of standing is only a custom. The riding incident is a small event (the rabbis do not stand, Abaye rebukes them, they explain) that is mainly speech, with some conflict and no change.
Courts ruled and collected from movable property, then Rav Nahman ordered them to reverse under threat; there are actions and conflict, but it is mostly rulings and a rebuke with no narrated outcome.
A one-line report of what Rava did (coerced Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity), cited as precedent with nothing following.
An incident is only alluded to in one clause as support for Ulla's ruling; nothing is narrated beyond the Sages' inability to release her.

Orphans come before Rava and he rules; the Sages challenge and he justifies it. Like Ketubot 50b:4, there is no narrated action or change beyond the ruling, and the exchange is ordinary halakhic debate.
Rav Sheshet compelled a divorce, the man tried to void it through the witnesses, and Rav Sheshet required a new bill: several actions, conflict and a response.
A bare report that Rav Haviva recited a blessing at a circumcision, followed by the Gemara's ruling; nothing follows from it.
Ben Yasiyan travels and finds a convert married to his brother's wife, then a dialogue in which he challenges him. Some action and a challenge, but it is mainly speech with no change.
A widow comes before Rav Yosef and he apportions food and wine; her retort about silk gives tension, but it is mostly a request-and-ruling exchange with little further action.
The rabbis buy sesame and hire sailors, the river is dammed, they make demands, and Rava rebukes them in court: several actions, conflict and resolution.
A woman challenges Rav Yosef with her own case and then confesses; the events are told only inside the dialogue, though there is conflict and a reveal.
Abaye's boast and a scholar's question lead into standard halakhic exposition: ordinary rabbinic dialogue with no event.
A husband complains, the bride explains, Rabban Gamliel investigates her relatives, confirms it and rules: several actions and a resolution.
The elders boycott the lecture, Rav Hamnuna is sent to ostracize them, fails their question, is mocked and returns to Rav Hisda: several actions and conflict.
The orphan daughters come before Shmuel, who rules; this is the Ketubot 50b case the expert ruled is not a story, with no narrated action or change besides the ruling.
A one-line report that Rav Shimi bar Ashi used the remedy on a gentile who was healed, cited to support the remedy; there is an act and an outcome, but barely a narrative.
A man sells land to Rav Pappa for oxen, no longer needs the money, and Rav Pappa returns the land: several actions and a change.
Rabbi Akiva mocks sinners, Satan appears as a woman, Akiva climbs the palm tree and Satan releases him: several actions, conflict and change.
Cases come before Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael, who rule, followed by scholarly discussion of the rulings; there is no narrated action beyond the ruling.
Part of the narrative of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's deathbed: he summons his sons, they enter and he hands over wisdom and the office of Nasi.
Mar Ukva's habit of secret charity leads to a one-time event: the pauper pursues them, they hide in a furnace, his legs are burned and his wife explains.
Part of the siege of Jerusalem narrative: Vespasian besieges, the wealthy pledge provisions, and the zealots burn the stores, causing famine.
Reish Lakish sells himself to gladiators, kills them by a ruse, escapes, and later lives and dies with no concern for wealth: several actions, conflict and change.
Judges rule, Reish Lakish reverses their decision and Rabbi Yohanan criticizes him; there is an action and a reversal, but it is close to a ruling followed by ordinary rabbinic criticism.
Ulla dies abroad, the news is brought to Rabbi Elazar, who laments, and they tell him the coffin is coming: events and a response.
Rav takes leave of Rabbi Hiyya, receives a cryptic blessing, searches and finds the verse, and it is borne out by his wife's behaviour: several actions and a change.
Rav Yosef son of Rava sets out home before Yom Kippur, his father comes out armed to meet him, they quarrel, and neither eats the final meal: several actions with conflict and consequence.
Geneiva passes by, the rabbis disagree over whether to rise for him, he approaches and teaches them; there are actions (passing, approaching) and a conflict beyond ordinary scholarly debate.
A narrated incident: a harvester is bitten by a snake and dies, his wife reports it, the court sends people who confirm it, and the Sages rule. An incident followed by a ruling.
An actual incident: a woman held as collateral in Ashkelon, her family distances itself, witnesses testify, and the Sages rule. Several actions and a resolution.

Rabbi Elazar's first-person account of testifying once, which led the court to (seek to) elevate a slave to the priesthood, has an action and a consequence; the Gemara's emendation in [3] is commentary (R-B4).
A full narrative: the debate on prayer, Rabbi's arrival, Rabbi Yishmael stepping over heads, the clash with Abdon, the yevama case, and Abdon's punishment, with conflict and change throughout.
A 'certain man' incident: he bequeaths his property to Toviya, dies, Toviya comes, and Rabbi Yohanan rules. Narrated events followed by a ruling, though very brief.
A couple comes before Rabbi; he sees their famine-blackened faces, has them bathed and fed, the husband then finds blood, and Rabbi rules. Multiple actions and a change.
General medical advice that Abaye passes on from his mother; there is no narrated event.
A woman comes before Ameimar, her brothers speak, and he stays silent; this is cited as evidence of his view, and no other action or change is narrated (the R-C0 limit, Ketubot 50b).
A certain woman holds deposited documents, the heirs demand them, she claims she seized them, and Rav Nahman rules. An incident with actions beyond the ruling, like the cow case.
The tumtum of Biri, who was operated on and later fathered seven children, is cited only briefly as evidence inside a legal argument; the incident is alluded to rather than told in full.
Within Rabbi's deathbed pronouncements is a story: the people of Bireta DeSatya catch fish on Shabbat, Rabbi Ahai excommunicates them, and they become apostates. Several actions and a change.
Bar Haddaya asks two authorities how to deliver a bill of divorce and gets different answers. It is consultation and speech with no further action or change.
A man holding orphans' coral assesses it for himself and takes it, it rises in value, and he comes before Rabbi Ammi, who rules. An incident with change followed by a ruling.
Ordinary scholarly back-and-forth: an objection and an answer passed down a chain of tradition. No event and no real conflict.

A woman writes her property over to her daughter to keep it from her husband, then marries and is divorced. Several narrated actions and a change; this is the opening of the story that is resolved in the next segment.
A certain woman holds deposited documents, the heirs demand them, she claims she seized them, and Rav Nahman rules. An incident with actions beyond the ruling.
Rav sends a halakhic question and Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi discuss it. Only quasi-speech acts, with no conflict or change.
The Sages allot wine to Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter-in-law, she blesses them, and they pointedly do not answer amen. An incident with a response.
Rav and Rav Yehuda are walking behind a woman and the passage is mostly their exchange about seclusion. There is some action and a mild challenge, but it is mainly speech.
Yehuda bar Mareimar is pushed to enter and sits silent, Abba of Sura misreads the silence and signs over everything he owns, and then retracts. Actions, conflict and change.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi is propositioned, covers himself with boils, is healed by magic, flees to a dangerous bathhouse and is protected by angels. A full story.

Rav Huna deliberately tears silk in front of his son to test whether he will become angry: an incident with intent and an implied outcome. The Gemara's follow-up questions in [3] are commentary (R-B4).
A woman signs her property away to evade a husband, marries and is divorced, Rav Nahman tears the deed, Rav Anan complains to Mar Ukva, who backs the ruling. Several actions and conflict.
Funerals became so costly people abandoned the dead, until Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in linen and everyone followed: actions with causal change.
Abaye rules for his tenant, Rav Yosef contradicts him, and Abaye runs three parasangs after the tenant without catching him: several actions and a change.
Two incidents in which a man does a judge a small favour (removing a feather, covering spittle) and the judge disqualifies himself: an action followed by a response.
Narrates a sequence of institutional changes (court raises widows' ketubah, grooms shun them, court reverts), with causality, but these are collective ordinances rather than a told incident.
Purely legal discussion of a mishna; no narrated event.
A woman obliged to swear in Rava's court, Rav Hisda's daughter testifies she is suspect, and Rava reverses the oath: an incident with an intervention and a ruling that changes the outcome.
A teaching exchange between Rav Yehuda and his son, speech only, with no conflict beyond a wry remark; the follow-up is Gemara analysis.
Only a remark by Rabbi Simlai to his host, cited as a proof, with no action or change; the rest is analysis.
A man betroths with a myrtle mat, is challenged, re-designates the four dinars, she takes it in silence, and Rava rules: an incident with several actions followed by a ruling.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa delays the Angel of Death, dies with a pillar of fire, and Rabbi Alexandri makes it depart: a full narrative with action and change.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak juggles myrtle at weddings, Rabbi Zeira objects, a pillar of fire marks his death, and Rabbi Zeira reverses his view: actions, conflict and change.
The couple's ketubah is lost and they come before Rav Yosef, who rules, is challenged by Abaye, and then orders a new one written: an incident with a change in the ruling and a resulting action.
After a habitual frame, a one-time event follows: Yehuda stays late, Rabbi Yannai declares him dead, and he dies.

The letter itself is speech and advice, but it embeds a short incident: a man who wanted to leave the Land for a woman heard this teaching and stayed, suffering until he died, which is action with a change.
A report of Rav Yehuda's practice and Ulla's advice; speech without conflict or change, followed by commentary.
Legal discussion that only alludes to the biblical David and Bathsheba incident; no story is narrated.
Scholarly argument over a halakha with no narrated event; normal rabbinic back-and-forth.
A bare report of where Rabbi lay ill and that he was moved, cited to reconcile two baraitot; nothing follows.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov goes to study, Abaye arranges for him to sleep in the study hall, and his prayer kills the seven-headed demon: a full narrative.
A man's testicle is pierced by a thorn and he later fathers children; Shmuel sends the case to Rav, who orders an inquiry. This is an incident with a response.
A man helps Shmuel off the ferry, reveals he has a case, and Shmuel disqualifies himself: an action, a response and a consequence.
Rabbi Evyatar meets Elijah and learns what God says of his interpretation. It is an encounter between a rabbi and Elijah (in scope by the R-S1 reading), though largely dialogue.
Ravina recites the blessing at the betrothal, confident the match will hold, and the family retracts: action and reversal. The Rav Tahlifa note is a bare report.
A beautiful woman claims to be betrothed to deter suitors, later betroths herself, explains herself to the Sages, and a ruling follows: several actions and a change.
A widow is refused by Rabba bar Rav Huna, curses him, he overturns his chair, and he still falls ill: conflict, actions and consequence.
Beyond the exchange, events are narrated: Rav Huna leaves, Rav Hisda speaks in his absence, Rav Huna returns, finds them and reacts with praise; actions and a change frame the teaching.
An incident (the daughter-in-law seized a bag of coins) followed by the Sages' inability to remove it; a narrated act with a response, the cow-case shape.
Full narrative of the Sages' visit to Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas and Akiva's encounter with Yonatan; segment 12 is the Gemara's halakhic commentary and is excluded.
A one-line corroborative report about a goat's missing spleen inside a list of remedies; no human protagonist, no response or development.
A narrated incident (a man willed a palm tree to his daughter, died leaving two halves) that leads to a dispute and ruling; the incident is the story.
Within the list of reports, Rav Aha bar Yaakov's illness, being hung from the column and cured is a narrated sequence with change, capped by his own account.
Rabba bar bar Hana loses a bill of divorce, offers identification, and it is returned; several actions and a resolution, followed by his reflection.
Mostly a proposal and a later objection (speech), but a narrated disruption (times of trouble prevented the enactment) and implied change make it more than plain dialogue.
At his son's wedding Rava pours drinks, some rabbis stand and others do not, and he becomes angry: actions, conflict and an emotional reaction.
The sharecropper is late, Rabbi Yannai tithes in advance, goes to Rabbi Hiyya, and recounts a dream that is interpreted; a narrated incident with ruling and resolution.
A widow comes before Rav Yosef and is apportioned support; beyond coming to court and rulings there is only a witty exchange, so at most borderline.
A man comes before the rabbis, they rule, and a colleague challenges with a baraita; coming before rabbis and being ruled on plus standard scholarly back-and-forth, with segment 3 as Gemara analysis.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tricks the Angel of Death, jumps into paradise, and meets Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai: a full narrative with many actions and change.
A man sold his property intending to go to Eretz Yisrael and did not go, and Rav Ashi ruled; an incident with actions followed by a ruling, the cow-case shape.
Two incidents of collapsing structures from which Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yohanan pull their helpers up, followed by the Sages' question and his answer; actions and change.
Rabbi Yehoshua is asked a halakhic question and answers with a testimony; pure speech with no conflict beyond scholarly discourse.
Rav Nahman's daughters and Rav Ilish are taken captive, he hears the birds, eavesdrops, escapes miraculously while his companion is killed; a full narrative.
A man comes before Rabbi Hanina to ask whether he may go down for levirate marriage and receives an answer; coming before a rabbi and being ruled on, with no other narrated action or change.
The heirs come before Rav Amram, refuse his advice, are threatened and sent to Rav Nahman who rules; several actions and conflict.
An incident (the daughter-in-law seized a bag of coins) followed by the Sages' inability to remove it; a narrated act with a response, the cow-case shape.
Rav objects, Shmuel's father is silent, Rav cites a verse; standard rabbinic dialogue, and segment 3 continues as Gemara analysis.
Two Rabbi Meir incidents: he stops the steward despite a dream, and he makes peace between two quarrelers after three weeks and hears Satan lament; actions and change.
The sons bought a maidservant, gave collateral, the price rose, and they came before Rabbi Ami who ruled; an incident with actions and change followed by a ruling.
Avimi's habitual honoring of his father leads into a one-time event (standing over his sleeping father until he woke) and a reward; habit plus event.
A woman seized a silver cup toward her ketubah, demanded sustenance, and Rava ruled; a prior narrated act and a ruling, the cow-case shape.
Narrated incident before R. Yohanan (two babies die, ruling) followed by Abaye relying on it, marrying Huma and dying: multiple actions and change.
R. Hama bar Bisa returns after twelve years, meets his unrecognized son, is distressed, stands before him; several actions, emotion and a revealing change.
Something happened (the boat sank with the scholars) and Rabbi responded by permitting the wives to remarry: incident plus ruling.
Rav Yosef son of Rava leaves study, his father confronts him with a weapon, both miss the pre-fast meal: actions, conflict and consequence.
Couple comes before Rabbi, he has them bathed and fed, blood is found and he rules: multiple narrated actions and a change beyond the ruling.
A rumor and a cited precedent ruling with no further narrated action or change; the incident is only alluded to as legal evidence.
Bar Kappara fails to rise, R. Shimon becomes angry and complains to his father, who responds: actions, emotion and conflict.
Mar Ukva's son reports the pauper's luxury and Mar Ukva doubles the gift; at death he reviews his records and gives away half his wealth: actions leading to change.
Ravina comes before Rav Ashi with a question and receives a ruling; no other narrated action or change beyond the ruling.
A report of Rav Ashi's blessing practice at a wedding, cited as evidence for the halakha; nothing follows from it.
Ketubot 15a:0: a legal discussion of an incident's facts, but not enough of the incident is narrated (expert ruled not a story).
A couple comes before Rav Yosef and makes claims; only the claims and (in context) a ruling, no further narrated action or change.
Purely a halakhic exchange between Rav Aha and Rav Ashi about a hypothetical deer; no event, no conflict beyond normal discourse.
A biblical incident (David and Bathsheba) only alluded to in a legal argument; no narration.
A teacher was negligent, Rav Aha made him vow to stop, Ravina reinstated him because no better teacher was found: several actions and a change.
Rava planned to expound the Name publicly and an elder objected; essentially speech with some conflict and implied change, so borderline at most.
Couple before Rabbi, he has them bathed, fed and given drink, blood is found and he rules: multiple actions and change.
A woman whose husband died in famine after she fled comes before Rava; the exchange causes Rava to change his ruling. Segment 3 is the ensuing legal conclusion.
Rabbis visit a town, are asked a question and debate it, then Rav Idi gives a ruling; standard scholarly dialogue without real conflict or change.
Renter disobeys the owner's instruction, the donkey dies, they come before Rava who rules: incident with actions followed by a ruling, like the cow case.
Ravin went as agent to betroth a woman for his son and betrothed her to himself: two actions and an unexpected change.
R. Tzadok is propositioned, stalls, climbs into the lit oven, and the noblewoman relents: clear sequence of actions with conflict and change.
Yehudit suffers in childbirth, disguises herself, asks R. Hiyya, drinks a sterility potion; later it is revealed and he laments: multiple actions and change.
A man deposits a goblet with Hasa, Hasa dies without instructions, they come before Rav Nahman who rules: incident with actions followed by a ruling.
A man sells land to Rav Pappa for oxen, ends up not needing the money, and Rav Pappa returns the land: actions and a change.
A certain man betrothed with a bundle of rags and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya examined its value before Rav: a narrated incident with a ruling. The Gemara's follow-up question is commentary.
Mostly question and answer, but he goes to a second rabbi and Rabbi Yehoshua mocks him sarcastically. That is speech with conflict.
A bare report that Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Ya'akov, followed by a halakhic statement. Nothing follows from it.
Two men quarrel over a city post, come before Rav Yosef, and he rules and assigns them roles: an incident with a resolution and a change.

Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok's account of bringing olives, their refusal and his father's response has several actions and causality. The mishna citation and the Gemara's inference that follow are commentary.
Rav Hisda's statement about his own early marriage is a dictum, not a narrated incident.
A brewer betroths with sediment, the owner finds him and comments, and he comes before Rava for a ruling: several actions plus a ruling.
A hypothetical legal dilemma about illness and menstruation; no event happened.
Rav Beivai arrives at Rav Yosef's house, eats, and has the ladder removed: a small narrated incident. The surrounding dicta and the Gemara's question are not part of it.
Only a fragment saying the Galileans sent a question. A quasi-speech act with no conflict.
A seating arrangement followed by a discussion, the same shape as the Yevamot 17a case the expert ruled not a story.
Buyers took the orphan's wine, its price rose, and the parties came before Rav Nahman for a ruling: an incident with a change and a ruling.
A bill of divorce is found, the Sages search from Sura to Neharde'a, and witnesses come and testify: several actions and a development.
Rabbi Yehuda bars Rabbi Meir's students, Sumakhos pushes in, Rabbi Yehuda grows angry and Rabbi Yosei responds: actions, conflict and emotion.
The relatives go back and forth between Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish over a stepmother's sustenance, with a threat and a resolution: several actions and conflict.
A Madonite seeks to give gifts, is advised, buys land, makes the gift, dies, and the Sages fulfil his words: a full incident.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa and the Angel of Death, the pillar of fire, and Rabbi Alexandri's pleas form a full narrative. The Abaye exchange at the end of segment 4 is commentary.
An old woman sells the orphans' ox, relatives challenge it before Rav Nahman, and the ox's value rises: an incident with a dispute and a ruling.
A habitual gift to a pauper, then one day the wife delivers it and reports he is not needy: a one-time event follows the custom.
The incident is only a statement that food became impure, followed by a ruling and a scholarly challenge. There is no other narrated action or change.
A man mortgages an orchard, it ages after five years, and the creditor comes before the Sages, who write him authorization: an incident with a change and a ruling.
A Roman courts a woman, makes her ill with pomegranates, then cures her for her consent: several actions and a change. The figures are post-biblical, so it is in scope.
A creditor seizes an ox from the orphans' herdsman, they dispute the timing, and they come before Rav Nahman, who rules: an action, a conflict and a ruling.
A man helps Shmuel off a ferry, reveals he has a case, and Shmuel disqualifies himself: action, consequence and change.
A Mishnah passage that is essentially Rabbi Zekharya's sworn testimony and the Sages' rejection. The event is only embedded in his speech, and it belongs to the Mishnah under R-C1.
Rabbi Meir's habit of mocking sinners leads to a one-time event: Satan appears as a woman, he crosses the rope bridge, and Satan releases him, so there are several actions and a change.
People call two men by a slur and a rabbi rules on each case. Apart from the ruling, nothing else is narrated as happening or changing.
Rav Nahman arrives and is asked a halakhic question, which he answers from a mishna. This is ordinary scholarly question and answer with no conflict and no event.

The scholarly exchange turns into an incident: Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin is embarrassed by a pun he misunderstands, and Rav Huna clears it up. Emotional reactions count as events, and the exchange contains a misunderstanding that gets resolved.
Rav Kahana is tempted, throws himself from the roof, Elijah catches him and then gives him money, so there are several actions and a clear change.
A report of Rav Ashi's practice with the wedding blessings, cited as precedent. Nothing happens beyond the practice and nothing follows from it.

Two conflicting deeds come before Rav Yosef, he rules, and the losing party protests and asks for a remedy. This is an incident plus a ruling, but beyond the ruling it is mostly courtroom speech with some conflict, so it is borderline. Segment 6 is the Gemara's commentary.
A sick-visit serves only as the setting for asking a halakhic question and explaining Rabbi Yosei's reasoning. This is standard rabbinic dialogue without conflict or change.
Rav walks among the sheaves and makes a remark to them, followed by Rava's saying. That is a single act plus speech, with no change and nothing that follows.
This is the Gemara's commentary on Rabbi Yaakov's incident, questioning whether it happened and why the man was harmed. It is not the story itself.
This is the opening of the incident of Rav Ashi, Mar Zutra and the king's food, which continues with actions and a resolution. The passage contains the start of a story.
