A report of what the Galileans habitually did for a poor man, followed by Gemara discussion. No one responds and nothing changes.

There is a small action (Rav Aha seats his granddaughter on his lap), but the substance is a mutual challenge over halakhic rulings, which is close to ordinary rabbinic back-and-forth, so it is borderline.
Abaye loses a donkey, messages go back and forth, and the Samaritans return it on account of his reputation, so there are several actions and a resolution.
This is the baraita's continuation of the Mishnah's Zekharya ben HaKatzav story, telling how he responded to the ruling. On its own it is a habitual arrangement rather than a narrated event.
A disputed virginity claim comes before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi, who runs a test with maidservants and a wine barrel and then rules. The incident has several actions and a resolution.

Mar Yehuda poses a contradiction, the others fall silent, they go to Rabba, and he calls the questioner quarrelsome. This is largely scholarly dialogue with some movement and friction, so it is borderline.

Yeimar bar Hashu has his agent seize the dead debtor's boat, and the rabbis confront the agent. The incident continues with them seizing the boat themselves, so there are several actions and conflict.
A fire breaks out at the wedding, the bride cries out, and people find the burnt body. That is a narrated incident, followed by the rabbis' deliberation on her testimony.

A renter disobeys the owner's instruction, the donkey dies, and the case comes before Rava for a ruling. This matches the incident-plus-ruling pattern of the cow example, with several actions and a change.
The Sages urge Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to marry and he deflects them, which is speech only. The Gemara then explains his real reason, which is commentary. There is no event and no real conflict.
A disputed virginity claim comes before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi, who runs a test with maidservants and a wine barrel and then rules. The incident has several actions and a resolution.
A report of what Rav Malkiyyu did for a deaf-mute neighbour, cited as precedent and praised by Rava. Nothing follows from it, much like the Mar Zutra case under R-C5.

While traveling, the rabbis twice see men sowing mixed seeds; one proposes excommunicating them and the other rebukes him. Beyond seeing, the passage is speech with some conflict, so it is borderline.
An exchange of letters causes offence: Rav Sheshet is sent with an insulting reply, Rav Anan goes to Mar Ukva and is rebuked. There are real conflict, several actions and a resolution.
A man brings R. Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing; he refuses it, seats other judges, and reflects on his own bias. Several actions and an inner change.
Homiletic exposition about fingers and ears; no event is narrated.
The Mishnah's Tzaidan incident is only cited with 'etc.', and then the Gemara asks about the Mishnah's structure. Nothing is narrated in this segment.
Aher sees Hutzpit's tongue dragged in the street, exclaims, and goes out to sin. A narrated event with a reaction and a change.
A chain of hypothetical halakhic dilemmas about Shabbat; no event.
A narrated wonder: an inherited mustard branch breaks, yields nine kav, and its wood roofs a booth. These are several events, of the eyewitness-wonder kind Jeff has accepted.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi sees huge grape clusters and curses the land. The next year the fruit has shrunk and the locals send R. Hiyya away. Actions and a consequence.
A bare report that R. Yohanan issued a ruling, followed by a Gemara question about terminology; no incident.
A divorcee comes before Shmuel and Rav Dimi tests her by passing her son along a row of women. The child recognizes her and she is ordered to take him.
Brief case reports (an immersion; men called 'son of an Aramean'), each followed by a ruling. No further action or change is narrated besides the rulings.
Rav Ashi at first does not remember, later recalls and testifies, and sees Rav Kahana hesitate, then reassures him. Several actions and an emotional reaction.
A teaching in the study hall, an objection from the audience and a clarification. This is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no event beyond speech.
Rav Hiyya Arikha's mother-in-law sues him for her ketubah. He ignores the ruling, an authorization to seize his property is written, and they appeal to Rava. A sequence of actions with conflict.
Rebbi falls ill, R. Hiyya visits and finds him weeping, and Rebbi explains why. Illness, a visit and an emotional reaction are narrated.
A man bequeaths his property to Toviya and dies, Toviya comes to claim it, and R. Yohanan rules. This is an incident with actions, resolved by a ruling.
A rumor and a question sent to Abaye, answered by a ruling. Nothing is narrated besides the rumor and the ruling.
R. Yohanan hears that the Habbarim have come, shudders and falls, then is told they take bribes and sits up again. These are events with emotion and change.
A ruling permitting the freed brothers to marry, then a scholarly challenge and a retort. No action besides the ruling, and the dispute is ordinary rabbinic discourse.
A one-line wonder cited as evidence: a fox nested in a turnip, which was weighed. It is minimal, of the open eyewitness-wonder type.
A man wishes to give away his movables, is advised, buys land and makes the gift, then dies, and the Sages uphold it. Multiple actions.
Mainly an exchange of teaching between R. Yohanan and R. Elazar, with conflict and R. Yohanan's grief leading to a consoling remedy. Speech with conflict is borderline.
A man brings a get to R. Yishmael and receives a ruling, then leaves. R. Elai enters and challenges, and R. Yishmael silences him. Several actions and a conflict.
A widow comes before Rav Yosef with escalating demands, he grants them, and she answers sharply. It is largely speech and rulings, with some conflict.
Avimi sends money with an agent, who pays and is refused the document, and the case comes before R. Abbahu. Several actions, a conflict and a ruling.
A divorcee comes before Shmuel and Rav Dimi tests her by passing her son along a row of women. The child recognizes her and she is ordered to take him.
A general halakhic ruling about kidnapped women followed by ordinary scholarly back-and-forth; no event that happened is narrated.
A woman comes before Ameimar, her brothers speak and he stays silent; cited as evidence of his view, with no further action or change beyond coming before a rabbi.
Rabbi Elazar testifies and the court acts on his testimony to elevate a slave, a narrated incident with a consequence; the Gemara's emendation in [3] is commentary revising the story.
A halakhic enactment and discussion, plus Abaye quoting his mother's teaching; speech and rulings only, no event.
A Jew and a gentile walk together, the gentile reminds him of the Temple, he sighs yet keeps pace, and they exchange words: several actions with a turn.
The prince's household seizes the orphans' maidservant, the judges sit, one approves and Rabbi Abba rebukes them: an incident with a ruling and conflict.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi arranges to irrigate Abaye's fields, tricks both sets of owners and dams the river, and Abaye refuses the produce: multiple actions and a change.
A witness narrates fleeing soldiers with Arye, who later died, and Rabbi Tarfon allows the wife to remarry: an incident followed by a ruling.
The widow sues the orphans, they object to her clothing, she dresses in all her clothes, and Ravina rules; several actions with a consequence.

Rav Pappa and Rav Huna intend to act, are corrected by an old woman and by Rav Pappi, and concede; mostly speech with conflict and implied change, plus an only-alluded strangling incident. [3] is Gemara commentary.
Rav Yehuda reports saying a ruling before Shmuel and Shmuel's disagreement: scholarly dialogue only.
Dama ben Netina's mother tears his cloak, strikes him and spits, and he does not shame her: several actions about a post-biblical figure.
A halakhic question and answer between Rava bar Rav Hanan and Abaye; no event.
A man makes a field a marker, contests it, dies, and his steward argues before Abaye, winning step by step and earning Abaye's praise: an incident with actions and rulings.
A gentile's threat reveals a killing, the wife goes to Abaye, who defers, is sent to Rav Yosef, and he rules: a sequence of actions and a resolution.
Funeral costs drove relatives to abandon the dead until Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in linen and everyone followed: an action that causes a change.
Ilfa hangs himself from a ship's mast with a vow, an old man comes and challenges him, and he answers: dramatic actions with a challenge.
Ravina arranges his son's match, recites the blessing early out of confidence, and the family retracts: actions and a reversal. The Rav Tahlifa note is a bare report.
Nehunya's daughter falls into the cistern, Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa reports her safe and she is rescued: a full miracle story. [4] is later comment on the story.
An actual incident is only alluded to as support for a ruling, and its details have to be reconstructed.
A pauper asks Rava for rich food and argues with him, then Rava's sister arrives with exactly that food and Rava concedes: actions and a change.
An incident (the master forced to free a half-slave woman) is cited only as a precedent, with its circumstances left to be filled in by the Gemara's conjecture.
Rabbi acts or intends to act, Perata objects, and Rabbi reverses: an incident with conflict and change, told in two versions.
Habitual generosity to the waiter leads to a change, Elijah speaking with one of them, matching Jeff's ruling on the parallel Ketubot 61a case.
A yevama spits before halitza, Rabbi Ami rules, Rabbi Abba challenges and suspects evasion, then goes out and finds a baraita: actions, conflict and a change of mind.

A man whose betrothed died comes before the rabbis, they rule, and Rav Hiyya objects; beyond coming for a ruling there is little narrated action or change, and the rest is a legal dispute (cf. the 50b limit of R-C0).
Rav's parting from Rabbi Hiyya, his wife's habitual contrariness, and the one-time event of his son reversing the requests, with discovery and response: several actions and a change.
A legal objection quoting a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about hypothetical cases; no narrated event.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi is propositioned, covers himself in boils, is healed by magic, flees to a dangerous bathhouse and is protected: a sequence of actions and a change.
Rabba bar bar Hana gives Rav money to buy land and Rav buys it for himself: two actions and a change; the Gemara's justification that follows is commentary on the incident.

An eyewitness account of Nakdimon's daughter, once rich, gathering barley from horses' hooves, with the sage's response in a verse; a narrated scene of change, though close to the open 'I myself saw' edge of R-C5.
Rabbi Zeira's sermon gets him pelted with etrogim; Rava preaches, is carried on silk, preaches again and is challenged: several actions with conflict and change.
A groom and bride dispute her virginity before Rabban Gamliel, who has the cloth brought, washes it, finds blood and rules: multiple actions and a resolution.
Mostly a negotiation in speech between brothers over a yevama and property; there is conflict and an implied change but almost no narrated action beyond the speaking.

Two incidents of men betrothing with items of doubtful value, each examined by a rabbi, the second with the mother's challenge and Rav Hisda's reply; the Gemara's reconciliations with Shmuel are commentary.
Pure dialogue between an Amorite and a resident of the Land, with a mocking challenge and a retort; conflict, but no event beyond speech.

The Nezonya elders skip Rav Hisda's lecture, Rav Hamnuna is sent to ban them, fails their question and is mocked, then returns to Rav Hisda: actions, conflict and change; the cited baraita in [5] is the legal answer, not narrative.
Legal analysis of a baraita on nursing vows; hypothetical cases, no narrated event.
A habitual frame (Rabbi Akiva mocking sinners) followed by a one-time event: Satan appears as a woman, he climbs the palm, and is released halfway.
After a habitual note, an incident where rabbis do not stand for Abaye and he rebukes them, answered with an excuse; mostly speech with mild conflict and no real change.
An amoraic inference and an objection from a mishna about hypothetical marriage-contract cases; no narrated event.

A man conditions a divorce on returning within thirty days, arrives but is blocked by the ferry, cries out, and Shmuel rules: incident with several actions plus a ruling; [3] is the Gemara's commentary.
A man sells himself to gladiators and comes to Rabbi Ami asking redemption; incident with actions and a ruling, though the passage is cut off and the ruling lies in the following context.
A mishna listing a wife's tasks and opinions about them; legal rules, no event.
King Yannai (a post-biblical figure) feasts, is incited against the Pharisees, is insulted, expels and kills the Sages until Shimon ben Shatah restores the Torah: a full narrative.
Rabba bar bar Hana recounts a man coming before Rabbi Yoshiya, who compels a divorce authorization and tells the elders to hide and write it: incident with actions beyond a ruling.
Rabbi Hama bar Bisa returns after twelve years, meets his unrecognized son, is distressed, then stands before him at home until his wife reveals the truth: actions, emotion and change.
Abba bar Marta repays Rabba in the Sabbatical year, takes the money back after Rabba's formula, Abaye intervenes, and the debt is repaid: several actions and a change.
A man instructs ten to write a divorce, two sign that day and the rest later, he comes to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi who rules: an incident with actions plus a ruling, though thin.
Mar Ukva writes about his tormentors, Rabbi Elazar replies twice, and Geneiva ends up in a neck iron: exchanges leading to a narrated change; [5] is a separate question-and-answer, not narrative.

Onkelos, a post-biblical figure, raises three figures by necromancy and questions them before converting; narrated actions with a consequence. Segment 7 is a separate dictum closing the Kamtza narrative.
An incident (Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebels and holds on to a garment), the sages rule, and Rav Gamda accuses them of flattery; the incident has actions besides the ruling, plus real conflict.
A baraita reports where Rabbi lay ill, and the Gemara reconciles it by explaining he was moved; this is a report and its harmonization, not a narrated story on its own.
Rav Sheshet exposes the Exilarch's servants, who then try to harm him; many actions, conflict and resolution.
An incident: Mar Zutra compels a rebellious wife to stay and from the couple R. Hanina of Sura is born; action followed by a consequence, though very brief.
R. Tarfon's habitual honoring of his mother leads to an event: he praises himself in the study hall and is told he has not reached half the obligation.
Rav Kahana gathers and eats dates a man knocked down; the man objects and Rav Kahana responds; actions with a response.
A habitual pattern (his wife aggravates him, he still brings her gifts) followed only by an exchange with Rav; conflict is present but no one-time event or change follows.
Orphans come before Rava, he rules, and the sages challenge him; as with the orphan daughters before Shmuel, no action or change is narrated beyond coming before a rabbi and the ruling.
A poor man asks Rava for charity and defends his luxurious diet; Rava's sister then arrives with exactly that food and Rava concedes; events with a change.
R. Eliezer enters the synagogue, finds no quorum, and frees his slave to complete it; several actions and a change, though cited as a proof.
Rabbi arranges a match, the bride dies, lineages are investigated, a new match is made and the son changes the terms twice; many actions and changes.
A report of R. Zeira's ongoing practice of avoiding Rav Yehuda, cited for a halakhic view; nothing follows from it.
Rav Pappa forces Yehuda bar Mareimar to enter; his silence makes Abba of Sura sign over all his property; actions, misunderstanding and change.
A rabbi states a ruling and is sharply rebuked; this is standard rabbinic dialogue, which the expert does not count as conflict.
A man who sold himself to gladiators asks to be redeemed; the sages report he eats forbidden food, and R. Ami sends him away; an incident with actions and an outcome.
Two brief case reports (a bequest whose price changed, then a ruling); no narrated action or change beyond the facts of the case and the ruling.
Rabbis stand for R. Shimon bar Abba as he passes and he explains why they need not; minimal action and a speech response, with no real change.
Pure dialogue in which an Amorite mocks the Land of Israel resident and is rebutted; speech with conflict and no other event.
A man asks Rav about his lineage, asks for his daughter, is refused, persists, and Rav's gaze kills him; actions, conflict and a dramatic change.
A baraita's hypothetical legal case and the Gemara's analysis; no event that happened.
Shmuel's instruction to gather ten men in order to announce a ruling is a speech act without conflict or narrated outcome.
A list of the scribes' letter-counts and a scholarly exchange about counting; ordinary dialogue, with no narrated event.
A hypothetical scenario built by the Gemara to explain a dispute; not an event that happened.
An incident only mentioned, in which Rafram pressed Rav Ashi into a ruling; a bare precedent report with nothing narrated beyond the ruling.
A man comes before Rabban Gamliel with a claim and the rabbi answers with a parable; beyond coming before the rabbi, nothing else is narrated and there is no real conflict (R-C0 limit).
A narrated incident with several actions and a change: the man sells two tracts, the creditor repossesses one, and the purchaser offers him money. Segment 4 is the Gemara's legal analysis.
Hanina declines the appointment, Afes presides, Levi sits outside, Afes dies, and Levi moves to Babylonia, where Rav infers what happened. These are a chain of events with change.
A question put to Abaye and his answer. This is speech only, with no conflict and no narrated event.
A brief wonder incident (a fox nests in a turnip, which is then weighed), cited as evidence. It is the kind of one-line Ketubot 111b wonder he accepted, though it sits on the open edge of R-C5.
The sages visit the sick Rabba bar bar Hana, a Persian priest takes their lamp, and Rabba reacts. Actions, conflict and an emotional response; post-biblical figures.
First-person reports cited as evidence for a halakha (a dish was brought and some was shared). Nothing follows and there is no change.
Rabbi falls ill, Rabbi Hiyya enters, finds him weeping and questions him. These are narrated actions with an emotional reaction, part of the deathbed episode.
A man snatches coins from another, throws them to a woman to betroth her, then comes before Rava, who rules. This is an incident with multiple actions followed by a ruling.
A pauper comes to Rabbi Nehemya, eats lentils with him and dies, and Nehemya laments. Actions, a change (death) and a reaction.
The mother writes two deeds, the two sons go to different judges who rule for each, and the judges confront each other. Multiple actions and real conflict.
A custom (meat bought daily for a poor man) with no one-time event or consequence following, plus the Gemara's commentary on it.
Rabbi Tarfon's eyewitness report (he went up and heard the High Priest) is cited as evidence for the baraita; nothing follows and nothing changes.
Exegetical discussion. Shmuel's instruction to Rav Hana is a cited speech-act with no narrated event or conflict.
Purely legal and exegetical discussion about the wedding benediction; no events are narrated.

A document is brought, Rav Pappa testifies and Rava rules, followed by ordinary scholarly back-and-forth. Apart from the ruling, there is no further action or change, and no conflict beyond normal discourse.
Rav Amram lifts the ladder, climbs, stops halfway, cries out, the sages come, and he expels his evil inclination. A full narrative with action, conflict and change.
A city's lineage is contested; Rabbi sends Romanus, who investigates and finds a convert girl, and Rabbi permits her. Several actions, ending in a ruling.

A man drowns and Rav Sheila permits his wife to remarry; Rav wants to excommunicate him, Shmuel advises inquiry, letters are exchanged, Sheila admits error, and the rabbis praise each other. Events, conflict and resolution.
A priest marries a convert girl, and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak confronts him and orders him to divorce her under threat. An incident with an action and real conflict, followed by a ruling.
A man studies twelve years, returns to find his wife infertile, Rabbi deliberates, and the husband prays and she is healed. Multiple actions and change.
Rav Yosef acts on Rav's ruling and Shmuel takes offense and rebukes him. A narrated act followed by an emotional reaction and conflict, though cited briefly as evidence.
A man sets a condition and later states that he tried. This is a legal case built from speech, with no further narrated action or change.
A teaching is heard and repeated before another sage, who gives a different tradition. This is transmission of teaching, i.e. speech, with no conflict beyond scholarly exchange.
A report that a question went unresolved for years until Rav Yosef resolved it; this is scholarly teaching with no narrated incident.
A report of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's habitual practice cited as evidence for a teaching; nothing follows from it and no change is narrated.
A man comes before Rabbi Hanina with a question and receives a ruling; per the R-C0 limit, coming before a rabbi and being ruled on is not enough without another narrated action or change.
Rabbi falls ill, Rabbi Hiyya enters and finds him weeping, and they exchange words; an actual event with action and an emotional reaction, cited as a baraita.
A man marks a field, contests it, dies, appoints a steward who argues before Abaye and wins, prompting Abaye's praise: multiple actions, a dispute, and a change.
A Mishnah stating a hypothetical legal case and a dispute; no narrated event.
Exegetical statements followed by a bare report of Rabba's and Abaye's lifespans; no narrated incident.
Rabbi Asi's relative asks him, then goes to Rabbi Yohanan who rules differently, and Rabbi Asi confronts Rabbi Yohanan: several actions and a real conflict.
The Gemara's commentary explaining Rabbi Akiva's conduct, not part of any narrative.
Rabbi Tarfon asks to be guarded, a student mocks him, and soon after the student sins with his mother-in-law: actions with a causal consequence.
A scholarly exchange with a jibe, plus a bare allusion to a wedding where oil was smeared, cited as evidence of custom; no narrated change.
A full incident: a fisherman lost in a cave is presumed dead, eulogized, and returns the next day; multiple actions and change.
Rami bar Yehezkel visits Benei Berak, sees a wonder and responds; an eyewitness-wonder incident of the kind the expert has accepted, though thin.
Abdan's daughters-in-law rebel, Rabbi sends Sages, they rebuff their husbands, and Rabbi rules: an incident with actions and a ruling.
A Mehoza woman comes before Rav Nahman, he recognizes her accent and rules, is corrected, and reverses his ruling: actions and change.
A visit framing standard halakhic question-and-answer between rabbis; ordinary scholarly dialogue without conflict or change.
Purely legal discussion of a baraita; no narrated event.
A document from Shmuel's court cited as legal evidence and explained; no narrated incident with action and change.
An incident in which one rabbi sought to give more than a fifth to charity and his colleague prevented him: two actions and a conflict, though brief.
A woman writes her property to her daughter to keep it from her husband, marries and is divorced: an actual incident with several actions that sets up a dispute.
Rav Asi's mother's demands, his departure, consultations with Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Elazar, and the arrival of her coffin: a full narrative.
Legal derivation about sustenance; no narrated event.
A report that a steward was selling land and buying oxen and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said nothing, cited as evidence of his view; nothing follows.
Homa comes before Rava, her arm is exposed, Rava goes home, and his wife drives Homa out of Mehoza: many actions, emotion and conflict.
The heirs come before Rav Amram, ignore his instruction, he threatens them and sends them to Rav Nahman: multiple actions and conflict beyond a ruling.
Ilfa hangs himself from a ship's mast as a challenge, an old man comes and tests him, and he answers: a dramatic incident with action and resolution.
R. Hanina bar Pappa's encounter with the Angel of Death, his death, the pillar of fire and R. Alexandri's intervention form a full narrative with many actions and change.
Ravina finds Mar bar Rav Ashi braiding a garland and questions him; one observed act followed only by a halakhic exchange, with little conflict or change.
Conflicting citations of Rava and a sarcastic retort are ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no narrated event beyond speech.
Rav Pappa's sister-in-law's levirate case: Abaye's ruse, the halitza, the dispute over payment, and Abaye's gaze causing the death of Rav Pappa's parents are narrated actions with consequences.
The Rabbis urge Rav Sheshet to marry and he replies; speech only without real conflict, and the explanation about his impotence is the Gemara's commentary.
The Exilarch's death on the road and the message sent, and the bill of divorce found in Neharde'a sent to R. Yehuda Nesia who ordered a search, are incidents with actions and responses.
A man left Pumbedita and Rav Yosef excommunicated him; another left and died, prompting Abaye's remark: brief incidents with action and consequence.
R. Elazar ascends to the Land, is ordained and appointed to the intercalation council, reacting at each stage: several actions and change.
Shimon HaAmasoni's withdrawal from his exegesis and his students' question is mainly about teaching and speech, with an implied change.
R. Elazar intended a ruling and a colleague advised against it; speech only, ordinary scholarly exchange without narrated action.
A woman before an unsuitable yavam performs halitza on a condition that is not kept, and R. Hiyya validates it: an incident followed by a ruling.
A man deposited sesame, demanded it back, and the bailee denied it; the dispute comes before the Sages, like the July cow case.
Rav Dimi bar Yosef places the divorcee among women, carries the baby past, and the child recognizes her: multiple actions and an outcome.
One partner frees half a slave, the other transfers him to his minor son to evade the court, and Rav Pappa devises a counter-ruse: actions, conflict and resolution.
Eyewitness wonders like R. Ya'akov ben Dostai walking ankle-deep in fig honey are the 'I myself saw' Ketubot 111b type the expert accepted in review and lists in 2005.
A brother's promise to split property, its breach, and the case sent repeatedly to different authorities form a narrated incident with conflict and multiple actions.
Levi intended to rule and Rav told him the halakha; speech only, no narrated action or conflict.
A relative sold her ketubba, was divorced and died, and the buyers claimed it from her daughter, prompting Rav Nahman's intervention: several actions and change.
A betrothal with a stone, the mother's claim and Rav Hisda's response, plus Yehudit's attempt to leave R. Hiyya, are narrated incidents with conflict.
Within Rabbi's deathbed pronouncements is a narrated incident: people trapped fish on Shabbat, were excommunicated and became apostates.
A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman, they disputed the timing, and came before Rav Nahman: an incident with action and a ruling.
A Mishnah reporting R. Elazar ben Azarya's exposition is teaching, a speech act, not a narrated event.
A son corrects his father's teaching and Shmuel rebukes him; it is all teaching and speech, with some interpersonal conflict over filial respect.
A half-free woman was treated licentiously and the court forced her master to free her: an incident with actions and change, though briefly told.
A will's instruction and a price change followed by a ruling; no further narrated action or change beyond the ruling.

Rabbi's match-making for his son: the bride dies, genealogy is investigated, a new match, the son marries early, studies twelve years, wife becomes infertile and is healed through prayer; many actions and changes.
A launderer who missed Rabbi's funeral throws himself from the roof and dies, and a Divine Voice grants him the World-to-Come; several actions and a change.
A slave flees to Eretz Yisrael, his master pursues him and comes before Rabbi Ami, who rules; an incident with actions besides the ruling, like the cow case.
The man only makes a stipulation and later claims he said a different date; speech acts with no further event, followed by legal analysis.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak's habitual juggling at weddings is criticized by Rabbi Zeira, and at his death a pillar of fire vindicates him; a habit that leads to a change.
Brief first-person reports of being given food at a meal, cited as evidence for a rule about waiters; nothing happens beyond the single act and nothing follows.

Rabbi Yohanan's relatives come to him, he advises them, and he later regrets having acted as a legal advisor; an incident with a change. The Gemara's explanation of his change of mind in [3] is commentary, but it shares a segment with his statement.
Dicta, then the Sages challenge Ben Azzai for not marrying and he answers; standard rabbinic back-and-forth with no narrated event.
A man makes a conditional divorce, comes back in time but is held up by the ferry, shouts across, and Shmuel rules; an incident with actions and an obstacle, followed by a ruling.
Mostly question and answer, though the widow's son goes from one rabbi to another and gets a mocking retort, so there is some conflict; still speech, so borderline at most.

Rav Anan's overfamiliar letter, Rav Huna's insulting reply carried under threat of excommunication by Rav Sheshet, and Rav Anan going to Mar Ukva; messengers and journeys with real conflict and consequence.
A groom complains he found no blood, the bride claims Dorketi lineage, Rabban Gamliel investigates her relatives, confirms it and rules; several actions and a resolution.
Rabbi Hiyya teaches a ruling under two attributions and the audience praises one and not the other; teaching and reaction only, cited to fix the halakha, with no conflict or change.
An eyewitness report that a woman came before Ameimar and he stayed silent at her brothers' words, cited as evidence of his view; coming before a rabbi with no other narrated action or change.
Rabbi's death: the Sages' fast and decree, the maidservant's prayers and the thrown jug, Rabbi's death, Bar Kappara's veiled announcement and Rabbi's last prayer; a full narrative.
A purely legal dilemma with no event.
An incident in Tzippori is only alluded to inside a legal discussion; not enough of the incident is told (the expert ruled this passage, Ketubot 15a:0, not a story).
After Mar Ukva's habitual gift comes a one-time event: his son reports the pauper's luxury, and Mar Ukva doubles the gift; habitual frame, then an event and a change.
A man brings Rav Anan a gift, Rav Anan disqualifies himself, then accepts and sends him to Rav Nahman, who misreads the letter; several actions with consequences.

The parents quarrel over whom their daughter should marry, the father gives in, and during the meal his relative climbs onto the roof and betroths her; [3] is the Gemara's legal commentary and is left out.
A man deposits silk with Rav Dimi, Rav Dimi dies without instructions, and the case comes before Rabbi Abba, who rules; an incident with actions and a change besides the ruling.

The orphans' relatives come before Rav Nahman with complaints about Amram the steward and he answers them; there is conflict, but it is almost all dialogue, and Amram's conduct is described only as a habit.
A tanner in Sidon dies, his brother the tanner is bound to levirate marriage, and the Sages rule that the widow may refuse; an incident with a ruling, though it sits in the Mishnah (R-C1).
The rabbis are about to rule and an old woman stops them by citing her own case, which is only alluded to; mostly speech, with some conflict and an implied change.
A baraita on yields and a Sadducee's remark to Rabbi Hanina about his land; speech only, with no conflict and no event.

Rav Hiyya bar Abba's child dies; Reish Lakish delays, then comes with his disseminator who offers words of comfort - a narrated sequence of actions. Segment 4 is the Gemara's commentary on the incident.
A yevama comes for halitza and Abaye hands over his left sandal, but the rest is a halakhic exchange between teacher and student; little action or change beyond the instruction.
Divine voice at Rabbi's funeral; the launderer who missed it hears, throws himself from the roof and dies, and a second divine voice declares his reward - multiple actions and change.
R. Hiyya bar Ashi's wife disguises herself as a prostitute, he propositions her, then sits in the oven and fasts all his life - a full narrative with actions and change.
A legal dispute between Rav and Shmuel about a deathbed gift; no narrated event.
Rav Hamnuna is sent to Rav Huna, who sees he lacks a head-covering, learns he is unmarried, and turns his face away - actions and conflict with consequence.
A woman comes to Jerusalem with a child, raises him, he has intercourse with her, and the court stones them - narrated events followed by a ruling.
The Madonite seeks to give gifts, is advised, acquires land, transfers the goods, dies, and the Sages uphold his words - several actions and a resolution.
A man deposits a goblet with Hasa, Hasa dies without instructions, and they come before Rav Nahman who rules - an incident with more than one action followed by a ruling.
Relatives seek rulings from R. Yohanan and Reish Lakish, are threatened by Reish Lakish, and return to R. Yohanan - multiple actions, conflict and outcome.
A groom complains to Rabban Gamliel, the bride explains, Rabban Gamliel investigates her relatives and rules - incident with actions and a resolution. Segment 3 is commentary.
An Arab woman brings phylacteries, Abaye lowballs her, she angrily throws them into the river, and Abaye regrets it - actions, conflict and change.
R. Zeira crosses the Jordan on a rope and is mocked by a Sadducee; mainly a dialogue but with conflict, matching the expert's borderline ruling on this kind of exchange.
Ulla visits Rav Yehuda and questions why his son is unmarried; the passage is mostly dialogue with interpretive digressions (3-5) and no narrated change beyond advice.
Avimi's habitual honor of his father, then one day his father dozes and Avimi stands over him until he wakes, and he is rewarded with insight - a one-time event with change.
In Neresh a betrothed woman is seated in the bridal chair and another man seizes her; Rav's students do not require a get - several actions and a ruling. Segment 3 is Gemara commentary.
A man conditions a divorce on returning within thirty days, arrives but is blocked by the ferry, calls out, and Shmuel rules - an incident with actions and a ruling.
Segment 2 concludes R. Hanina bar Pappi's story; segment 3 narrates R. Tzadok, the noblewoman, and his sitting in the oven - full narratives with actions and change.
Rabbi's deathbed instructions, his posthumous Shabbat visits ending when a neighbor learned of them, and his attendants dying before him - narrated events; segments 3-5 and 9 are Gemara commentary.
Conclusion of the incident: his friends shunned him and called him a name, and Rabbi elevated him to priesthood on his word - actions and change.
An account of rabbinic ordinances about cups in a mourner's house and their later reversal - institutional history rather than an incident about particular people.
Elijah's dietary advice to R. Natan is a bare speech-act with no event or conflict.
Rabbi Yannai rebukes Rav Hanina for a halakhic statement - ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no further action, which the expert does not count.
R. Elazar poses a halakhic question to an elder; a speech-act with no narrated event or conflict.
A halakhic dictum about soldiers of David's wars writing conditional divorces, with exegesis; no narrated event.
Mar Ukva's secret charity: the pauper sets out to discover him, they flee into a furnace, his feet are burned while his wife's are not. Several actions and a change.

Two narrated incidents: a man drowns and his body is pulled out days later, then a rabbi permits his wife to remarry. Under R-C0 an incident followed by a ruling counts, and here the drowning and recovery are actions besides the ruling.
A narrative about Nebuchadnezzar, Pelatiah ben Benaiah and the prophet Ezekiel. These are biblical figures, so it is outside the collection's scope.

A sharecropper betroths a woman with onions taken from the field and comes before Rava, who rules. Like the cow case, there is an act besides the ruling; the Gemara's added qualification is commentary.
Two one-line first-person anecdotes (food is brought, the master shares it), cited as evidence for a law. Close to the open eyewitness-report edge of R-C5, so borderline.
Purely legal argument (a dictum, an objection, an answer) with no narrated event.

A Jew and a gentile on the road: the gentile reminds him of the Temple's destruction, the Jew groans but keeps walking fast, and they exchange words. A narrated incident with actions and a resolution.
A bare report of Rav's practice of sustaining orphans with wheat, followed by legal analysis. Nothing follows from the act.
A man sells land to Rav Pappa to buy oxen, ends up not needing the money, and Rav Pappa returns the land. Several actions and a change.

A husband travels to collect his wife's inheritance, spends his own money, takes one dinar of hers, and comes before Rabbi Ami, who rules and is challenged. An incident with actions besides the ruling.
Bare reports of how many wedding blessings two Sages recited, cited as evidence of practice. Nothing follows.
Ilfa hangs himself from a ship's mast, vowing to fall if he cannot answer a challenge; an old man comes and challenges him, and he answers. Dramatic action and a resolution.
People come before Rabbi Ami and he rules. Per R-C0's 2026-10-07 limit, being ruled on is not enough without another narrated action.
Legal discussion of hypothetical claims; no event is narrated.
The Gemara's commentary on the preceding incident (whether it happened, and the man's thoughts). Under R-B4 commentary is not part of the story.

Rav Giddel's land is bought by Rabbi Abba, complaints pass up a chain of rabbis, there is a confrontation and an offer, and the land ends up abandoned as 'the land of the Sages'. Multiple actions, conflict and change.
A Mishnah incident in Sidon: a tanner dies, his brother is also a tanner, and the Sages rule the widow may refuse him. It belongs to the Mishnah under R-C1, but it is a narrated incident.
A dying man's bill of divorce, Rava's ruling, Rav Ilish's challenge, Rava's embarrassment, and the discovery that she was betrothed. Segment 6 is the Gemara's commentary and is excluded.
Dama ben Netina will not wake his father, loses a sale, and is rewarded with a red heifer. A post-biblical figure, a full story with action and change.
A poor man demands fine food from Rava; Rava's sister then arrives unexpectedly with exactly that food, and Rava concedes. Conflict, events and a change.
Rabbi Oshaya stays silent at Rabbi Yohanan's question but answers Reish Lakish, and is challenged for it. Mostly speech and quasi-speech acts with some interpersonal tension, so borderline.
Part of the deathbed narrative of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the Sages are summoned and come in, and he gives his final instructions. A narrated event within a larger story.
Rabbi Akiva and ben Kalba Savua's daughter: a secret betrothal, her father disowns her, Akiva studies for twelve years and returns with students. A full story.
A customary frame, then a one-time event: the sharecropper comes early with his case, Rabbi Yishmael refuses the gift, appoints judges, and catches himself rooting for the litigant. Story.
A man frames his wife with egg white to avoid paying her marriage contract; Bava ben Buta exposes the trick and the man is flogged and made to pay. Segment 4 is later commentary and is excluded.
Rabbi Ami declares a neighbor a mamzer, the man goes about weeping, and Rabbi Ami responds. That is several narrated actions and an emotional reaction.
The Exilarch's household mistreats Rav Amram, he tricks them, and Yalta rescues him in the bathhouse. That is a sequence of actions with conflict and change.
A man sets a condition, comes back on time, is held up by the ferry and calls out, and then Shmuel rules. This is an incident followed by a ruling, with narrated actions besides the ruling.
One rabbi passes on a teaching and another replies with a different version of it. This is ordinary scholarly exchange of speech, with no conflict or change.
A man comes before Rav Nahman with a claim and Rav Nahman rules that he be flogged. Coming before a rabbi and getting a ruling, with no other narrated action or change, is not enough.
This only reports a habitual practice of buying meat daily for a poor man, with nothing following from it. The rest of the passage is the Gemara's commentary.
Rav Sheizevi is laughed at and Rava rebukes those who laughed. It is speech only, but the mockery is conflict that goes beyond ordinary back-and-forth.
These are general dicta about sending a child to school. No event is narrated.
The boat is seized by Yeimar's agent and then by the two rabbis, Rav Pinehas challenges them, and Rava rebukes them. That is multiple actions, conflict and a resolution.
This is a legal objection and its answer. Nothing is narrated.
Two men trade insults, which is speech only but contains conflict. Segment 2 is the Gemara's legal framing, not part of the incident.
The rabbis intend to act and an old woman stops them by alluding to her own earlier case. The past incident is only mentioned and the present one is mostly speech, though it changes their course.
The Sages award Nakdimon's daughter-in-law her allowance, she blesses them, and they pointedly do not answer amen. These are several actions and responses.
The incident of the widow who removed her husband from the grave is only alluded to and has to be filled in from the commentaries, which is Jeff's case for R-C6. The rest is legal discussion.
A woman arrives with a child and raises him, he has relations with her, and the court stones them. These are narrated events followed by a ruling.
It reports a single act, sending Rabbi a gift of fabrics, followed by an explanation of the terms. There is no response, change or continuation.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba sees Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing his grandson to synagogue and asks why, and from then on changes his own practice. That is action, encounter and change.
This is a full story of Solomon, Benayahu and Ashmedai. Its characters are biblical, not rabbis or post-biblical figures.
Ulla dies abroad, the news is brought to Rabbi Elazar, and he laments and then answers the objection that the coffin is coming. These are events with an emotional response.
A man comes before Rav Nahman and is ordered flogged, which is a ruling without any further narrated action or change. Segment 3 is the Gemara's commentary.
The rabbis are served a huge peach and divide it, and a year later Rabbi Elazar finds the fruit shrunk and responds. These are several actions with a change.
The owner rents out a millstone, becomes rich, buys his own millstone and demands payment, and the renter refuses. This is a narrated incident with change and conflict.

Hasa's death is announced, Rav Nahman reacts, and the wife remarries without objection, with an alternative version of the same incident in segment 3. Rav Ashi's inference and the closing comment are commentary.
A beautiful woman fends off suitors by claiming to be betrothed, later betroths herself, and explains herself when the Sages question her. This has multiple actions and a change.
This is a one-line wonder report of a fox nesting in a turnip that was then weighed, cited as evidence. It sits on R-C5's open edge between a bare report and an incident.
A legal clarification of the mishna about a groom whose wife menstruates; no event is narrated.
A Roman courts a woman, makes her ill by eating pomegranates in front of her, then cures her once she agrees: several actions and a change, about post-biblical figures.
One rabbi praises a ruling and another rebukes him for it. This is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, which Jeff ruled is not a story (Ketubot 21b:0).
A man comes up and kisses Rabbi Yonatan's foot, and the explanation narrates how Rabbi Yonatan forced the man's sons to support him: several actions and a change.
A debtor sells two mansions, the creditor seizes one and goes after the other, and the buyer comes with money and an offer: an incident with several actions, followed by legal discussion.
Legal analysis of the difference between two Sages' opinions; no event.
Rabbi rules (or intends to rule) on an incident, Perata objects, and Rabbi reverses himself: actions and a change. Segment 3 is a variant telling of the same incident.
Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai meets Nakdimon's impoverished daughter, recognizes her and weeps: a full narrative with actions and an emotional change.
Rav Asi's elderly mother makes demands, he leaves for Eretz Yisrael, she follows him, he consults the rabbis and sets out, then learns she has died: many actions and a change.
A ruling plus a remark that an incident happened that way. The incident is only alluded to, not narrated.

An eyewitness account: the woman sees the rabbis, throws down her spindle and speaks to Rabba bar bar Hanna, and Rav Ukva comments. Several actions in sequence. The closing dispute over what he said is Gemara commentary.

A man sends a bill of divorce, the agent is prevented from delivering it and comes to Rava, Rava rules, is challenged and is embarrassed, and the facts then come to light: actions, emotion and a change.
The house of the prince seizes the orphans' maidservant, the court approves, and Rabbi Abba accuses the judges of currying favor: an incident with real conflict and a ruling.

A man comes before Rav Nahman with a claim and Rav Nahman rules he should be flogged. Coming before a rabbi and being ruled on, with no other narrated action or change, is not a story by Jeff's 50b ruling.

Rav Hiyya bar Abba's child dies, Reish Lakish delays and then comes with his disseminator, who delivers words of comfort: a narrated event with actions. Segments 3, 4 and 7 are Gemara commentary, excluded under R-B4.
A bare report that Rav Pappa instructed someone in line with his ruling, with nothing following.

A wife brings two maidservants into the marriage, the husband takes a second wife and gives her one of them, the first wife cries out before Rava, and he ignores her: several actions and a change. The interpretation that follows is commentary.
A rumor and a ruling to suppress it. No narrated action or change beyond the ruling.
The house of the prince seizes the orphans' maidservant, the court approves, and Rabbi Abba accuses the judges of currying favor: an incident with real conflict and a ruling.
An incident is mentioned only as the occasion for a legal derivation. Nothing is narrated.
A mother deeds her property to two sons on the same day, two judges each rule for a different son, and the judges then confront each other: several actions with conflict.
Rabbi Pinehas plans an escape, makes his declarations, is carried off and pursued, and the investigation that follows is halted: a full narrative.
Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's escape from Jerusalem and his meeting with Vespasian: a full narrative. Segments 11 and 12 are the Gemara's commentary.
A man testifies before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who rules on a man's Levite status. Coming before a rabbi and receiving a ruling, with no other narrated action or change, is not a story.
A widow sues the orphans, they ask her to dress properly, she puts on all her clothes, and Ravina's ruling then counts those clothes against her: several actions with an ironic change.
An incident: a woman obligated to swear, Rav Hisda's daughter testifies she is suspect, and Rava reverses the oath — narrated events with a response and change.
A report of what Rav Safra and Rava habitually did, cited as evidence for a halakha; nothing follows.
A habit frames a one-time event: the sharecropper comes early, Rabbi Yishmael refuses the gift, appoints judges and reflects on his own bias.
A man assesses orphans' coral for himself, it appreciates, and he comes before Rabbi Ammi who rules — an incident with actions and change followed by a ruling.
Rav Pappa forces Yehuda bar Mareimar to enter, his silence causes Abba of Sura to write away all his property, followed by the exchange — multiple actions and change.
A couple comes before Rava, who places an intermediary, then a scholarly exchange; little narrated beyond coming to court and a ruling, though Rava acts on what he observes.
A full narrative: agents fetch a vessel, are tormented, one tells them to hit the other, and Rabbi Ahai judges their conduct.
An encounter on the road leads mainly to a dialogue between Rav and Rav Yehuda; little action beyond the speech, with some tension.
A habitual practice (maidservants greeting Rabbi Abbahu with song) with no one-time event or consequence.
A city of slaves is sold, their masters die, they come before Ravina who rules and defends his ruling — an incident with change followed by a ruling.
Rabbi Zeira's sermon leads to his being pelted with etrogim; Rava's sermons lead to his being carried on silk and then rebuked — actions, conflict and change.
An incident (the Yavne reservoir found deficient) followed by the rabbis' dispute that ends with Rabbi Tarfon conceding to Rabbi Akiva.
A bill of divorce is found in Rav Huna's court, Rav Hisda sends Rabba to investigate, and he goes, examines and finds the source — narrated actions with a result.
The incident behind Rava's ruling is only alluded to in a sentence (a man hid his money as a gentile's and was forced to sell); it is not narrated in full.
A brief incident: in the race to Jerusalem the daughters beat the sons and were found eager and the sons lazy — a one-time event with an outcome.
A man grabs coins from someone, throws them to a woman to betroth her, and comes before Rava who rules — the cow-case shape of incident plus ruling.
A habit frames a one-time event: Rabbi Hanina's wife delivers the charity, discovers the pauper's luxury, and Rabbi Hanina reacts.
Marta bat Baitos sends her agent repeatedly for flour, goes out herself, steps on dung and dies — a full narrative of post-biblical figures.
Elijah departs from Rav Anan after his error, Rav Anan fasts and prays, Elijah returns frighteningly, and Rav Anan builds a box — actions and change.
A man studies twelve years, his wife becomes infertile, Rabbi deliberates, and the husband prays and she is healed.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov is afflicted, suspended from the cedar, expels a green substance and is spared impotence — actions and change; the list of others is a bare report.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seize an orphans' cow, receive conflicting rulings from Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish, and return to him — actions and conflict.
The note about King Shapur's daughter is a brief report of a habitual practice cited as evidence, with no narrated change or consequence.
A husband travels to collect his wife's inheritance, spends his own money and takes one dinar of hers, then comes before Rabbi Ami who rules and is challenged.
An incident only alluded to within a legal argument: Rav Yosef ruled like Rav and Shmuel took offense and mocked him; conflict but little narrated.

A certain man's sold mansions are repossessed, the purchaser offers a thousand dinars, and Rava rules; an incident with several actions resolved by a ruling. Segments 6-7 are the following legal discussion.
Pure legal exegesis about a yavam and teruma; no event is narrated.
A man threw a bill of divorce to his wife and it fell onto a board; Rav Yosef rules. A narrated incident with more than one action, followed by a ruling.
Burial expense drove relatives to flee; Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in linen and all the people changed their practice. Action leading to change.
Rabbi Natan asks Sumakhos a legal question and receives an answer; speech only, no conflict or event.

Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel imposed excessive fear on his household, which led them to try to feed him a limb from a living animal; an embedded incident with cause and consequence, though the Gemara reinterprets it.
The passage only cites the Tzaidan incident by its opening words and asks why the mishna mentions it; the incident itself is not narrated here.
Rav Avya's wife lost her marriage contract and the couple came before Rav Yosef; part of a narrated incident with an event (the loss) and a ruling that continues.
The Nehardean insults Rav Yehuda, is excommunicated and declared a slave, summons Rav Yehuda to Rav Nahman, and the confrontation unfolds; multiple actions and conflict.
A difficulty unresolved for twenty-two years until Rav Yosef became head of the academy and resolved it; mainly about scholarly teaching, with little narrated action.
A hypothetical legal case (if the father delivered her and she was widowed on the way), not an event that happened.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi returned home every Shabbat eve after death; once a neighbor knocked, the maidservant revealed him, and he stopped coming. A habit leading to a change.
Rav Hiyya bar Abba's child died; Reish Lakish delayed, then came with his disseminator who delivered words of comfort. Narrated events and actions.
Two brief first-person reports of a dish brought and shared with the attendant, cited as evidence for a rule; minimal incident with only implied consequence.
Rabbi Akiva and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter: betrothal, banishment, twenty-four years of study, return, and the father's vow annulled; a full story.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi attaches himself to the afflicted, then tricks the Angel of Death and enters paradise where he meets Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai; many actions and change.
Dama ben Netina's mother tore his cloak, struck him and spat at him among Roman nobles, and he did not shame her; a post-biblical figure, several actions and conflict.
A bare report of how Ravina collected a dowry, cited as proof for a legal point; nothing follows.
Part of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's deathbed narrative: he summons his sons, they enter, and he transmits wisdom and the office of Nasi.
A fragment of exegesis about the Israelites eating after the omer; no rabbinic story, and the event is biblical.
A report of what Rav Kahana did with an orphan's beer and his reasoning, cited as practice; nothing follows.
Shimon HaAmasoni's habit of expounding every 'et' ends when he withdraws, and his students question him; mainly about teaching and speech, with one change.
A sharecropper betrothed a woman with onions taken from the field and came before Rava, who ruled; an incident with actions followed by a ruling, like the cow case.
A man deposited pearls with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without instructions; the parties came before Rabbi Ami, who ruled. Several actions and a resolution.
Rav Pappa intended to rule leniently, was challenged by Rav Huna, and refrained; mostly scholarly dialogue with a small implied change.

The Beitar custom is the frame for a one-time event: the emperor's daughter's attendants cut a cedar, residents beat them, the emperor attacks. Segments 3-4 are exegesis and aftermath statements, not narrative.
Rabbi Meir's habit of mocking transgressors leads to a one-time event: Satan appears, he crosses the rope bridge, and is released halfway; multiple actions and a change.
Describes a government decree and the Gemara's legal analysis of it; no particular narrated incident.
The incident of the Rokhel mother: she was ill, gave instructions, died, and the Sages fulfilled her words, with Rabbi Elazar's reaction; an incident followed by a ruling.
A legal statement by Rav Huna and its analysis; no narrated event.
A man states where he is from and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha comments on it; speech without conflict, followed by legal discussion.
Ulla dies abroad, the news is brought to Rabbi Elazar, who laments and responds when told the coffin is coming; events, emotional reaction and response.
A son-in-law passed his in-laws' door amid rumors and Rav Sheshet flogged him: an act and a response, but cited in a line as a challenge with little narrated.

Embedded in the letter is an incident: a man lovesick for a woman wanted to leave the land, heard this teaching, and suffered there until his death; actions and change. The rest of the letter is advice.
A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, Rav Dimi died without instruction, the case came before Rabbi Abba who ruled; an incident with actions followed by a ruling.

Rabbi Abba buys land Rav Giddel was negotiating for, complaints escalate, a confrontation at the festival, the offer of a gift, and both refuse it so it becomes 'the land of the Sages'; multiple actions, conflict and resolution.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi visits Gavla, sees huge clusters and curses the land; the next year they have shrunk and the locals send Rabbi Hiyya away; actions and a change.

Gardeners settle accounts, one is told to give the surplus to the landowner who acquires it, he later recalculates and goes to Rav Nahman who rules; an incident with multiple actions followed by a ruling.
Dama ben Netina, a post-biblical figure, refuses to wake his father and forgo a profit, and is rewarded the next year with a red heifer; actions, causality and change.
Bar Shatya sold property, two pairs of witnesses contradicted each other, and Rav Ashi ruled; an incident with actions and a ruling, though cited as precedent.
A document is brought to Rava and the exchange is almost all speech, but it carries a personal edge, since Rava says he trusts Rav Hisda's daughter more than his own student.
A habitual practice of what Rava would say to such fathers; speech with no one-time event.
A man comes before Rabbi Hanina with a question and receives an answer; coming before a rabbi and being ruled on, with no other narrated action or change.
Two deeds come before Rav Yosef, he rules, and the losing party protests; a court case that is mostly ruling and dialogue, but there is conflict.
A debtor sells two mansions, the creditor seizes one and then the other, and the buyer goes to him with money and an offer; multiple actions and conflict.
A widow comes before Rav Huna, is refused, takes an oath on her own initiative, and the ruling changes; conflict and change, but it is all speech acts and a ruling.
Rabbi Pinhas plans his escape, makes his statements, is carried off and chased, and the others investigate lineages until it becomes dangerous; multiple actions, conflict and change.
Exegesis followed by ordinary scholarly challenges and answers; standard rabbinic dialogue, not a story.
The Elders in Lod debate study against action and reach consensus. It has a narrative setting, but it is speech only and ordinary scholarly disagreement with no event.

Rabbi's deathbed instructions, his returning home on Shabbat eves until the maidservant revealed him and he stopped coming, and his attendants dying before him are narrated events with change. Segments 3-5 and 9 are the Gemara's commentary.
A man sends a divorce via an agent, the wife (kneading) appoints the agent instead, and the case is sent from rabbi to rabbi with a stringent outcome; several narrated actions and a resolution.
A habitual return home is broken one day, R. Yannai's words cause Yehuda's death; habit followed by a one-time event and a dramatic change.
A bare report that Rav Haviva recited a blessing at a circumcision, cited for the halakha; nothing follows.
Ze'eiri avoids R. Yohanan's marriage offer, carries him over water, and R. Yohanan confronts him; actions with conflict.
Tzafenat bat Peniel is abused, put up for sale, and cries out to God; a full post-biblical narrative. The Jeremiah exegesis in [5] is commentary.
The blind man's lateness, the messenger's errand, the adultery report and Shmuel's ruling form a narrated incident with several actions before the ruling.
Rava and his wife exchange words about gossip concerning her; speech only, with some conflict.
Two incidents of collapsing structures where R. Abbahu and R. Yohanan rescue their supporters, followed by the Sages' question; narrated events with change.
A woman comes to a rabbi and he apportions support; coming before a rabbi and being ruled on, with no other narrated action or change (as in Ketubot 50b).
An incident only cited as a precedent (Rabbi gave one-twelfth) with no narrated action beyond the ruling.
Orphan daughters come before Shmuel and he rules; Jeff ruled this passage (Ketubot 50b) not a story — no other action or change.
A one-line eyewitness wonder (Rami bar Yehezkel sees milk and honey); the expert accepted the Ketubot 111b wonders in review and lists them.
Kamtza and bar Kamtza: humiliation, informing, the blemished offering and the Sages' indecision; a full narrative. R. Yohanan's comment in [8] is commentary.
Rav's examination of a family is only alluded to within a halakhic discussion; nothing narrated follows.
Rabbi goes to study with R. Elazar ben Shamua, the students gang up on him and he learns only one thing; actions, conflict and consequence.
King Yannai's feast, the provocation, and the killing of the Sages; a full narrative about a post-biblical figure.
Rabban Gamliel serves drinks at his son's wedding, R. Eliezer refuses and R. Yehoshua accepts, followed by an exchange; actions with conflict.
Yevamot 107b, Pishon's wife: one act mentioned without change or causality, explicitly ruled not a story.
Incident with a narrated event (a girl sweeping is attacked by a dog) followed by Rabbi's ruling, like the stolen-cow case.
Pure halakhic dialogue between Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa with no narrated event.
The Neharde'an man insults Rav Yehuda, is excommunicated, summons him to Rav Nahman's court, and the trial ends with marriages annulled and an attempted stoning; a long narrative.
An explanatory history of ordinances on marriage-contract sums, collective and generic, offered to reconcile sources, not a narrated incident about particular people.
Mar Ukva's habitual charity is followed by a one-time event: the poor man pursues them, they hide in a furnace, and an exchange with his wife.
A minimal medical anecdote cited for a remedy: Ravin treated Rav Ashi's daughter and she was healed; there is a change but barely narrated.
A single act (betrothing with vegetables in the market) followed by a ruling, with no other action or change.
A deposit, the custodian's death without instruction, and a hearing before Rabbi Ami form an incident with a ruling. Segment 3 is the Gemara's comment on it.
Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef finds Rabbi Abbahu, asks, and learns the teaching forty times. This is mainly rabbinic teaching and speech, which the expert ruled borderline.
The rabbis visit, a huge peach is brought, and they divide it. A year later the fruit has shrunk and Rabbi Elazar reacts: several actions and a change.
A drought, the mass sale of houses and the arrival of wheat are narrated events and a change, followed by Rav Nahman's ruling.
A narrated incident: a man recalls his childhood immersion for teruma and his friends' taunts, and Rabbi elevates him to the priesthood on that basis.
The wedding custom is the frame for a one-time event: soldiers seize the birds, a fight and a war follow, bar Deroma dies, and the massacre comes.
A man mortgages his orchard, it ages (a change), the creditor goes to the Sages and they issue a repossession document: an incident with a ruling.
Apart from the bare frame of travelling and meeting an elder, this is a halakhic question-and-answer exchange: speech without real conflict or change.
Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai meets Nakdimon's impoverished daughter, they talk and he weeps: a full story. Segment 5 is the Gemara's commentary.
Rav Huna tears silk to test his son, but the son's response is not narrated and the rest is Gemara commentary. A single act with an implied outcome.
A gentile's offhand announcement of a death leads Rav Yosef to let the wife remarry. Apart from the reported death, the narrated material is speech and a ruling, close to the expert's 50b limit.
The passage is only the opening fragment of an incident, a man saying something to his heirs. No event is narrated within it.
Rabbi Elazar ascends to the Land of Israel, is ordained, then is appointed to the intercalation council, and responds at each step: successive events with change.
A legal dispute among tannaim and amoraim about teruma allotments. Nothing is narrated.
A wife brings maidservants, the husband marries a second wife and gives her one, and the first wife cries out before Rava, who ignores her: several actions, conflict and a resolution.
Analysis of the mishna's wording. There is no narrative.

A man comes before Rabbi Ami and testifies, Rabbi Ami questions him and elevates the other man to the priesthood. This is mostly testimony and ruling, close to the expert's 50b limit, though the elevation is a change.
A gentile's offhand announcement of a death leads Rav Yosef to let the wife remarry. Apart from the reported death, the narrated material is speech and a ruling, close to the expert's 50b limit.
A man betroths a woman with a myrtle branch in the market, the case is sent to Rav Yosef, and he rules flogging and a divorce: a narrated incident with a ruling.
Incidents with narrated events (travel, death, burial reported by a gentile), after which the Sages allow the wives to remarry.
A legal dispute about a hypothetical case between Pumbedita and Mata Mehasya. There is no narrated event.
Mar bar Rav Ashi buying a cloth above its value is a bare report of one act, cited as evidence, with nothing following.
A man transports purification waters, a corpse fragment is found in the boat, and the Sages issue a decree: an action, a discovery and a response.
A man sells his property intending to emigrate and Rava rules on it. The subsequent change (not going, wanting to renege) is only implied, so there is little beyond one act and a ruling.
A drought, the mass sale of houses and the arrival of wheat are narrated events and a change, followed by Rav Nahman's ruling.
A testamentary instruction, a price change and a ruling; no narrated action or change beyond the ruling.
A man betrothed with a myrtle branch in the market, the case was sent to Rav Yosef, who ordered him flogged: an incident followed by a ruling with consequence.
The incident is only alluded to; what is narrated is Rafram pressuring Rav Ashi into a ruling and collection, thin but with some action.
Bar Shatya sold property, conflicting witnesses came forward and Rav Ashi ruled: an incident with actions followed by a ruling.
Gittin 43a: public teaching, challenge and public retraction via an interpreter; mostly speech, ruled low confidence at most.
A man comes before Rabban Gamliel with a claim and receives a parable in reply; essentially speech with implied conflict and no further action.
R. Hanina declines the appointment, R. Afes dies, Levi leaves for Babylonia and Rav deduces it; segment 4 is the Gemara's commentary.
A document brought before R. Abbahu and R. Yirmeya's correction is ordinary scholarly exchange with no further action or change.
An incident merely alluded to as precedent in one line; not enough of the incident is given.
Ravina comes before Rav Ashi with a question and receives a ruling; no other narrated action or change.
A halakhic objection citing a mishna; no event is narrated.
Akiva's students died, the world was desolate, until he taught the southern rabbis who upheld Torah: events with change; segment 4 is added commentary.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi's exclamation causes the fruit to shrink, as the next year's visit shows: actions with a consequence.
R. Hananya leaves for twelve years, returns, finds his home, his wife dies of shock and is revived by his prayer.
Legal discussion of defects in slaves; no event narrated.
Levites leave a sick companion at an inn, the innkeeper reports his death and his wife is allowed to remarry; a Mishnah story, catalogued as such.
The elders in Lod debate study versus action; speech only, with a disagreement and a resolution.
The girl dies when the contract is written, the lineages are checked, a new match is made, the groom shortens his study and is ashamed before his father.
A maidservant immersed, a bone was found in her teeth, and Rabbi required another immersion: an incident with actions and a ruling.
A sick man wishing to give his property acquires land, makes the gift, dies, and the Sages uphold it.
A man acted on tracing witnesses' names in ordinary documents and Rav Kahana had him flogged: an act with a consequence.
Rabba bar bar Hana brings a document before R. Elazar and receives a ruling; no other action or change.
R. Hiyya bar Ashi's wife disguises herself, he propositions her, sits in the oven, learns the truth and fasts until death.
A description of R. Abba's habitual charity practice with no event or change following from it.
Legal statements and analysis about a groom's claim; no event narrated.
Ravina arranges his son's match and recites the blessing early, confident; the family then retracts - actions and a reversal. The Tahlifa line that follows is a bare report.
The Titus narrative (a post-biblical figure): desecration, the sea storm, the gnat, his death. Interspersed exegetical comments (4, 6, 8) are Gemara commentary.
R. Hiyya bar Abba visits Gavla, sees violations, stays silent, then reports to R. Yohanan, who orders a proclamation - several actions followed by a ruling.
A report of what Rav Kahana did with an orphan's beer, cited as practice; nothing follows from it.
The Gemara only cites the mishna's incident by its heading and then derives laws from it; the narrative itself is not told here.
The teacher is absent, is questioned, recounts the miraculous harvest, and Reish Lakish rebukes him - events with consequence.
A sharp scholarly retort about who first taught a ruling - ordinary rabbinic dialogue with no event.
A certain man sets a condition, tries to appease his wife and fails; Rav Yosef rules - incident with actions followed by a ruling.
A woman sells her ketubah, is divorced and dies; buyers claim from her daughter and Rav Nahman intervenes - multiple events and a response.
The death of Rabbi: the decree, the maidservant's prayer and the thrown jug, his death, Bar Kappara's announcement - a full narrative.
Two rabbis on the road see men sowing mixed seeds and debate excommunicating them; little happens beyond the exchange, though it responds to an observed event.
Rav Aha sends his son, decides to go himself, Abaye arranges for him to sleep in the study hall, and he kills the demon - many actions and change.
Peleimu's habitual taunt leads to a one-time event on Yom Kippur eve where Satan tricks and confronts him - a full story.
Rabba bar bar Hana gives Rav money to buy land and Rav buys it for himself - two actions with a consequence; the justification that follows is Gemara commentary.
A hypothetical legal case from a baraita, not an event that happened.
Opening of the Rav Ashi and Mar Zutra episode at the king's gate, which continues into a narrated incident with actions and a miracle.
Cases that came before Rabbi and R. Yishmael are only mentioned as precedent rulings, then discussed; no narrated action beyond the ruling.
Reports of Abaye's and Rav Sheshet's practices and a brief question-and-answer with Rav Kahana; no conflict or change.
Shmuel's maidservant is captured, redeemed and sent to him with a message - several events, resolved by his response.
The carpenter's apprentice schemes to take his master's wife, leading to divorce, remarriage and the master's humiliation - a full narrative.
A couple comes before Rav Nahman, who rules by her accent and revises when told of the husband's town; coming before a rabbi and a ruling, with no further narrated action.
Rav Ashi fails to recall, later remembers and testifies, notices Rav Kahana's hesitation and reassures him - actions and change beyond dialogue.
